Texto do anúncio: My neighbor got home from work on a Tuesday in June and started emptying his savings account. Not all at once. A little every few days, the way you would if you didn't want anyone asking. He sold the boat. He told his daughter she wasn't going back to school in the fall. His wife thought he was leaving her. He told me the real reason over the fence on a Sunday morning and I have not slept properly since. That was six weeks ago. I still haven't told my son. But I've already done every single thing he said. His name is Ray. Sixty-one. Runs the overnight crew at a plant two counties over. Twenty-six years there. The dullest man on this street and I mean that kindly. We've lived beside Ray and Denise since 2011. Fourteen years. He mows in straight lines. He waves with two fingers off the wheel. In fourteen years I have never heard that man raise his voice about anything, including the time my dog got into his tomatoes. Which is why I noticed. It started with the boat. That boat sat on his driveway for nine years. He was never going to use it and we all knew it and it was a running joke on this street. In June it was gone in four days. Then Katie didn't go back to school. Then Denise called me on a Thursday morning crying. "He's taking money out of the bank. Cash. He won't say what for." I said something useless. I think I said men get funny at that age. "I think he's got somebody," she said. I didn't believe that for a second. But I didn't have anything better. Then on Sunday morning I looked out of my kitchen window and saw Ray doing something I had never once seen him do in fourteen years. He was digging. Not gardening. Digging. Shovel, boots, a pile of dirt beside the shed, hole already past his knee. Ray pays a boy to do the heavy yard work. Ray does not dig. He'd been at it about an hour. No radio. No water bottle. Just digging. I watched him for a while from the sink. Then I poured two coffees and walked out to the fence. "Ray." He looked up. "I brought you a coffee." He put the shovel down and came over. Wiped his forehead with his sleeve. "Thank you." "Ray, what in the world are you doing back there?" "Putting some things away." "Away." "That's right." "In a hole." "That's right." I laughed a little. He didn't. "Denise called me Thursday. She was crying." That got him. He looked down into his coffee. "I know she did. She told me." "She thinks you're leaving her." "I know." "So what are you actually doing?" He didn't answer right away. He looked off past his shed at the tree line. I waited. I'm good at waiting. "You know I can't really talk about work." "I'm not asking you about work." "Everything I'd tell you right now is work." I didn't say anything to that. "There've been a lot of meetings this spring," he said. "That's all it is." "All right." "Some of them have been hard to sit through." So I tried it another way. "Ray. What are you getting ready for?" That one was different. He took a long breath in through his nose. "You watching the news? The shipping lane?" "The Strait. Everybody is. You can't fill a tank any more without wincing." He nodded, slow. "That's the part they're letting you see." "Meaning what?" "Meaning the price of gas is the surface. The meetings I've been sitting in are about what gets decided because of the price of gas. And that part isn't on the news yet." "What part?" He was quiet a second. Then he said, "You remember 2020?" "Which bit?" "The bit where somebody else decided which stores you were allowed to walk into. How far you could drive. How many people could sit in your own living room." "I remember." "They did it once and it worked. They know how now." I felt something go cold across my chest. "They know how to do what?" "Same thing. They'll just give you a different reason for it." "Ray." "Fuel first. Cards, limits per household per week, you prove you've got somewhere worth going. Hospitals get theirs, trucking gets theirs, everybody else waits in line." "That doesn't happen here." "It's happening somewhere else right now. It just hasn't gotten here yet." "All right." "Then it's power. An hour here, three hours there. Please don't run your dryer between two and seven. And you'll do it, because what else are you going to do." "Ray, stop." "I'm not trying to frighten you." "You're doing a heck of a job anyway." He almost smiled at that. Almost. "So what do I do?" I said. "Buy a generator? Fill the pantry?" And he laughed. A tired little laugh, not a real one. "Everything you just said. The pantry. The cash. The boat. Katie coming home. All of that is the easy part." "Easy." "That's what anybody who's lived through a real shortage would tell you to do. Anybody over eighty who remembers the seventies. Anybody in my line of work who's been watching this build since March. That's not insight. That's just homework." "Ray, you are burying money in your backyard. That is not homework." "It is to the people who know." I let that sit. "So then what is it," I said. "What's the thing keeping you up?" He turned the coffee cup around in his hands. "It's something I worked out sitting in a meeting I probably shouldn't have been in. Nobody outside that room is saying it out loud yet. And I'd trade everything in that hole for it if somebody made me choose." "Ray." He looked at me. "Water." "Water?" "When this lands, water is the thing. Not gas. Not cash. Not what's in your freezer." "Water." "You can go a long time without food. You can go a good while cold. You cannot go long at all without clean water, and the second every household in this country works that out on the same afternoon, it's over." "Over how?" "The water aisle goes first. Then Costco. After that there's no water for sale anywhere at any price. You're drinking what you put back or you're not drinking." "But the tap." "The tap's the part nobody sees coming." "The tap's fine." "The tap is a supply chain. It's power, and it's chemicals that arrive on a truck, and the truck runs on the diesel we were just talking about. Every step between the river and your kitchen has somebody else's problem in it. When one of them wobbles, you get a notice telling you to boil your water." "So you boil it." "On what?" I didn't have an answer for that. "If the reason the water's bad is the power," he said, "then your stove's out too. So now you're boiling water on a grill in the yard with whatever propane's in the tank. For how long? Three days? Three weeks?" I said, all right, but how often does that actually happen. And I expected him to have a number ready, because Ray always has a number ready. He shook his head. "I'm not giving you a number." "Why not?" "Because you'd take my word for it. And you shouldn't take anybody's word for it, including mine, including whoever's selling you something next week." "Ray." "Go inside. Type in your own county and the words boil advisory. Not the state. Your county. Then read what comes up and make your own mind up." So I did. That evening, at my own kitchen table, on my own laptop. I'm not going to tell you what I found, because you should go and do exactly what I did. It took me four minutes. I'll only say I stopped thinking he was having a breakdown. Here's the part I actually sat down to write about, though. Because the fuel and the hole in the yard is not why I'm typing this at eleven at night. The following Sunday I went back out to the fence and asked him whether I should be buying water. He said something I wasn't expecting. "Water you store is a number that only goes down." "Meaning what?" "Meaning you can stack that garage to the roof and all you've bought is a countdown. Two weeks. Four if you're careful and you stop washing. Then it's gone, and the tap is still bad, and there's no truck coming." "So what do you do instead?" "You quit storing water and you get something that makes it." Now I'll be straight with you. Standing there I was sure a sales pitch was coming. Forty years of church suppers and school fundraisers teaches you to hear one coming. People go slightly polite right before they want something off you. It didn't come. He said "hold on," went in through his back door and came out with something in his fist. Held it up. "This." "That's a pen." "It's a filter. You drink through it. Or you screw it onto a bottle." "Ray, that's nothing. That's the size of a marker." "That's the point of it. It goes in a drawer. It doesn't want power. It doesn't want a refill. And it doesn't go off sitting there." "And that works?" "You're going to ask me that again in about four minutes. Put your shoes on." There's a creek behind our houses. There's been a creek behind these houses since before either of us moved in. It runs down past the back of the Hendersons' place toward the culvert. It is brown. There is a tire in it. Nobody has ever thought about that creek for one second in their life. He crouched down at the edge and filled an empty bottle straight out of it. I want you to understand what that water looked like. Not tea-colored. Brown. There were things turning over in it. I would not have washed a car with it. He screwed the little tube onto the neck of the bottle and squeezed some out into a mug I'd carried down with me. What came out was clear. Then he drank some. Standing in the mud in his Sunday shoes, in front of me. Then he held it out. "You first," I said. "I just went first." So I drank it. I'm going to be careful here because I don't want to sell you something I didn't get. It tasted like water. That's all. Regular water, cold because the creek was cold. There was no grit in it. It didn't smell like anything. There was nothing about it that made me want to spit it out on his shoes. I pulled the bottle back and looked at it. The water in the bottle was still brown. What had come through was clear. I said something I won't write down. He turned it over and told me how it works, and I wrote this down when I got home because I wanted to get it right and because I knew nobody would believe me otherwise. There are two parts to it. The first part is the straining. He gave me the number, a hundredth of a micron, and that meant nothing to me standing in a creek. What it means in plain words is it catches the bacteria and the muck. The second part is the one he said nobody talks about, and it's carbon. Carbon is what pulls out the chemicals and the taste. "The first part is why it's safe," he said. "The second part is why a child will actually drink it. Most of the cheap ones only do the first part. So it's technically safe and it tastes like the bottom of a pond, and then your grandbaby won't touch it, and you're right back where you started with a screaming child and no water." That was the sentence that got me. Not the micron. That one. I asked how long one lasts. Eighteen hundred gallons. And it doesn't expire sitting on a shelf, which is more than I can say for the case of water in my basement with 2019 on the side of it. "Buy it once," he said. "Put it in a drawer. Forget about it until the day you can't." He put the one from his hand into mine. "Take that. I've got more. I'll bring some over tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Don't make a production of it. They don't need to understand it. They just need to have one when it matters." Then he went back to his hole. Here's what I did about it. I walked back up from the creek, got in my car to go to the store, and then sat in it on my own driveway for about ten minutes without starting it, if you want the truth. Because nobody tells you what it's like to be the one who finds out first. My son Marcus is forty minutes away. My daughter is two states over. There are eleven houses on this street and I know every person in nine of them. Nancy across the street is eighty-three and she has nobody. And I sat there doing arithmetic in my head about how many I could afford. Not how many I needed. How many I could afford. I'm seventy-two. Bill is seventy-five. We are not people with money. Every dime counts in this house and has since he retired. And I remember thinking, very clearly: I do not have enough water to help this whole street. Ray dropped a bag on my porch Monday morning. Didn't knock. Just left it. I drove to Marcus's on Tuesday and gave him three. One for him, one for Amy, one for the truck. I mailed two to my daughter with a note that said don't argue with me. I walked one across to Nancy and told her it was a spare. My son-in-law rolled his eyes at me. I watched him do it, right across the kitchen table. I don't care. He can roll his eyes. Denise has stopped worrying about Ray, by the way. She keeps one in her purse now. Now listen. I'm not going to sit here and tell you the world is ending. Ray never said that, and I'm not going to say it on his behalf. What he said is that there are more moving parts between the river and your kitchen tap than anybody realizes, and when one of them stops, the entire plan is a piece of paper telling you to boil water you have no way of boiling. That's it. That's the whole thing. If you've had a feeling these last few weeks that something is off, and the news keeps going around it without landing on it, you're not making that up and you're not being dramatic. The people who know are getting ready. Quietly. They're not making announcements. This is the one Ray put in my hand over that fence. I've put the link underneath. 👉 tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial EDITED TO ADD: I did not expect this to go anywhere. It has not stopped since Thursday. Two ladies from my Tuesday group. My cousin in Ohio. A woman I have not spoken to since Bill's surgery. All asking me the same thing, which is where do I get one. The link is up above and it's the only place I know of. It isn't in the stores here. I checked two of them before I ever went out to that fence, which tells you how much attention I was paying. Don't take my word for any of it, by the way. Go and read what it does. I didn't take Ray's word for it either, and he's the one who handed it to me. I'd rather tell you that than have you find out later I'd dressed something up. P.S. I finally told Marcus the whole thing, start to finish. Including the part about the grill. He listened the whole way through without saying a word, which is not like him. When I finished he asked me one question. "How far's the nearest water from you?" I'd already worked it out. Four hundred yards, the creek. He didn't ask anything else, and two days later Amy texted me a photo of theirs in the glovebox. P.P.S. I asked Ray what he'd say to somebody who thinks all this is a bit much. He said: "Ask them what their plan is. Not what they're worried about. Their plan." I've asked four people that now. Nobody's had one. I didn't have one either, six weeks ago. P.P.P.S. One of them does eighteen hundred gallons. I had to look up what that meant. It's years, for one person, out of a creek or a rain barrel or the tub you filled the night before. Nothing to plug in and nothing to replace. That's the part I'd want somebody to tell me. P.P.P.P.S. And if you're sitting there thinking you'll just buy the jugs instead, go back and read what Ray said about the countdown. Stored water runs out. That isn't a criticism of storing water, I've got a basement full of it, it's just arithmetic. Being able to make water safe does not run out. Fourteen years of knowing a man and it took him ten minutes in a creek to explain the difference to me. 👉 tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

Texto do anúncio: My neighbor's husband came home from a work trip to Washington last month and started quietly shutting his family's life down. Sold the bass boat he spent six years fixing up. Cancelled the Alaska cruise for their 35th anniversary. Moved money out of the bank. Talked his son into hauling the grandkids back from Phoenix. His wife was sure a doctor had given him bad news and he was hiding it from her. He told me the real reason over our back fence, and it came down to one word. That was three weeks ago. I still haven't told my husband. But I've quietly done every single thing he told me to do, before the rest of this street figures it out. His name is Warren. 61 years old. Thirty-four years in fuel logistics. The steadiest man I know. I've lived next door to Warren and Marlene for 14 years. Our grandkids run through the same sprinkler. Warren leaves Monday and comes home Thursday. Houston mostly. This year, a lot of Washington. Doesn't say much. Waves from the mower. You ask him something, you get the answer and nothing extra. In 14 years I have not once seen that man rattled. So when he started acting odd in August, I noticed. First it was the boat. Then the cruise. Marlene had that brochure on her fridge since Christmas. Then the bank. She found the withdrawal slips in his jacket pocket. Then a moving truck pulled in from Phoenix. Their son Kyle, his wife, two little girls and the dog. Into the basement "for a while." Nobody would tell her why. Then the deliveries started. Plain brown boxes. A whole pallet one time. Straight into his shop with the door pulled shut behind him. Marlene sat at my kitchen table on a Wednesday and cried. "He's sick. I know he's sick. He got some kind of news and he's putting his affairs in order and he won't tell me." I didn't know what to say to her. Then Saturday morning I was at the sink, looked out my kitchen window, and saw Warren doing something I have never seen him do in 14 years. He was splitting firewood. Two cords at least, dumped beside his shop. Warren out there in his work shirt with a maul, swinging. Warren and Marlene have gas logs. They've had gas logs since the day they moved in. He'd been at it better than an hour. No radio. No gloves. Just swinging. I stood there and watched him a good 20 minutes. Then I poured two coffees and walked out to the fence. "Warren." He stopped. "Brought you a coffee." He looked at the maul. Looked at the pile. Looked at me. Then he leaned the maul on the stump and came over. "Thank you." "Warren, what on earth are you doing?" "Getting some wood in." "Wood." "Yep." "For the gas logs." "Wood stove's coming Thursday." I laughed. He didn't. "Warren. Come on now." "It's a stove. People have stoves. It's no big thing." "A box of candles is no big thing. You've got a lumber yard back there." I nearly got a smile out of him. "Marlene thinks I've gone off the deep end." "Marlene thinks you're dying. She sat at my table Wednesday and cried about it." That one got to him. He looked down in his cup. "I know. She asked me straight out that night." "She thinks you've got six months and you won't tell her, Warren." "I know." "So what is it really." Nothing. He drank some coffee. Looked off past his shop at the tree line. I waited. "You know I can't talk about work." "I didn't ask about work." "Anything I've got to say right now is work." I kept my mouth shut. "I've sat in a lot of rooms since the spring. That's all it is." "All right." "A few of them I'd have paid good money not to be in." I came at it another way. "Warren. What are you getting ready for?" That one he felt. He let out a long breath. "You been following the oil thing? The strait?" "Hormuz. Sure. Gas is ridiculous again. It's all anybody talks about after church." He nodded slow. "That's the piece you're allowed to watch." "Meaning what." "Meaning the news shows you the ships. The rooms I've been in aren't about ships. They're about what gets done here, at home, once fuel gets short enough. None of that's been on your TV." "What gets done." He went quiet again. Then: "You remember 2020?" "Which part." "The part where somebody decided which stores were essential. Where they told you how many people could sit at your own table at Thanksgiving. Where two weeks turned into a year." "I remember." "Well, they kept the binder. All of that got built once and nobody took it apart." I went cold right down both arms. "Kept it for what." "For this. Same binder. New reason." "Warren." "Fuel goes first. They won't call it rationing, they'll call it a conservation order. So many gallons per household per week. Odd and even days by your license plate. Military and hospitals fill up first, then farms, then trucking. You and me get what's left and a line to stand in." "That doesn't happen in America." "It did happen in America. 1973. You and I are both old enough to remember our dads sitting in those lines. And it's happening right now. Slovenia started rationing gas in March. Fifty liters a day. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency that same week. We're not at the front of the line. But we're in it." "Okay." "Then trucking. Diesel goes where they say it goes. Store shelves get thin, then patchy. Flights get cut and they'll blame prices." "Okay." "Then the power. Plants get told to throttle back. Brownouts. An hour. Then an afternoon. Kindly don't run your air conditioner between two and seven." "Warren." "And 2020 had an end because a virus runs its course. This one runs until the oil moves. They signed a deal in June and it was dead in three days. The truce fell apart in July. The Navy's cleared better than a hundred suspected mines out of that water and the ships still won't go. There's one pipeline across Saudi Arabia that gets oil around the strait. One side door, and everything is leaning on it. Nobody in those rooms is talking in weeks." I just stood there. "That's why Kyle and the girls are in my basement. That's why the boat's gone. That's why there's a stove coming Thursday." "All right. So what do I do?" He looked at me a while. Then he sort of laughed. A worn out laugh. "Tell you the truth, everything I just listed is the easy part." "Easy?" "It's what your grandmother would've done without anybody telling her. Anybody who sat in a gas line in '73. None of it takes inside knowledge. It's chores." "You sold a boat you loved, Warren. Don't stand there and tell me that's chores." "It is to the people who know." I didn't answer him. "None of that is what has me up at three in the morning." "Then what does." Long drink of coffee. "Something that came up about a month in. One slide, in a room I only got into because somebody was out sick. They spent four minutes on it and went on. I'd give up every box in that shop before I'd give up my answer to it." "Your answer to what?" He looked right at me. "Water." "Water?" "When this gets bad, clean water is the whole ballgame. Ahead of cash. Ahead of a full tank. Ahead of that wood pile." "Water." "You can be hungry a good while. You can get through a cold house with blankets. You get about three days without water. And the day every household in the country works that out at the same time, it's done." "Done how." "Austin, Texas, 2018. One boil notice. The stores were out of bottled water in hours. Hours. And that was one city, with the trucks all running and the rest of the country to pull from. Now do every city at once with diesel on a conservation order." "But we've got the tap." "The tap goes too. Nobody ever sees that one coming." "Warren." "Water gets to your house because electric pumps push it there. Pumps lose power, the pressure drops, and when the pressure drops, whatever's in the ground around those old pipes can get pulled inside them. That's why they tell you to boil. I didn't make that up, it's in the EPA's own guidance." "Texas, February 2021. Grid went down in the cold. Over fourteen million people had their water knocked out or messed up. Some of the boil notices ran past a month. The man who ran the state's own environmental agency told a reporter he was on day four with no water at his house. Him, his family, his dog and eight chickens." "Fourteen million." "Fourteen million. From a cold snap. Asheville after the hurricane, fifty-three days before they could drink from the tap. Jackson, Mississippi, close to seven weeks. Richmond, Virginia, January of last year. One power outage at the water plant and the whole city was boiling water." "Every one of those was weather. One place at a time. With the whole rest of the country standing by to send trucks." "What I'm telling you about is everywhere at once. And nobody's standing by, because everybody's in it." He set his cup on the fence post. "Picture it. Your grandbabies are thirsty. The store's empty. The tap's running brown, or it isn't running. There's no truck coming because the truck has no diesel. And you're stood in your kitchen trying to work out what goes in the sippy cup." "Don't." "I know. I'm sorry. But that's the one that gets me up at night. Everybody's staring at the gas pump. Nobody's looking at the faucet." "This can't be right." "Ask yourself why every headline says oil and not one of them says water. The folks in those rooms know how this goes. They won't say it out loud, because the minute they do, the water aisle is empty by supper. That's what 'avoiding a panic' means." "All right. So what are you doing about it?" He looked at his cup. "We're covered." "What's that mean." "Means we're covered." "Warren." "I'd rather leave it there." "You haven't left one thing there in twenty minutes." Nothing. "Warren. You just stood my granddaughter in my kitchen with an empty sippy cup. You do not get to say that to me and go back to chopping wood." He looked at me a long moment. "It's not something I'm meant to be passing around." "Passing what around." "What people in my line of work are doing at their own houses." "Tell me." He sighed. Looked at the shop. Looked at the wood. Looked back at me. "There's an item. One particular item. Everybody I trust in this business has them. The fella who runs our Gulf terminals. A woman on my team who did twenty years in the Coast Guard before she came to us. My boss ordered ten back in the spring, for his kids and the lake place, when all anybody else was buying was gas cans." "What item." "It's small. It's cheap, considering. It's no secret, you could look it up tonight. It's just that nobody outside my little world has tied it to any of this yet." "Warren. What is it." One more long look. Then: "Stay put." He went in his shop. Came back out with something in his hand. Black tube. Maybe nine inches. About the size of a flashlight. He held it up. "This." "A flashlight?" "A water filter. A straw, they call it. You can drink through it straight out of a pond. Or it threads onto a regular water bottle, any standard one. Rain barrel. Creek. The bathtub you filled before the pressure dropped. No batteries. Nothing to plug in. One of these is good for 1,800 gallons." "And that's what..." "That's what we've all got. There's one in Marlene's glove box, she just doesn't know what it is. One in each of the girls' backpacks. That's the item." "That little thing." "That's why it works. Goes in a purse. Needs no power and no refills. And nobody can put it on a conservation order." "Warren, does that thing actually work?" "I'll let you answer that yourself in about five minutes. You got an empty water bottle in your recycling? Go get it." I went and got one. Plain store water bottle out of the bin. Followed him around the back of his shop. There's a rain barrel back there under the downspout. Been there since before we moved in. Nobody's cleaned it in years. Brown. Leaves rotting in the bottom. You wouldn't let a dog drink out of it. He took the lid off. Took my bottle. Pushed it down under the surface and let it fill. It came up the color of old dishwater with bits turning over in it. Then he threaded the straw on where the cap goes. Handed it to me. "Drink." "Warren." "Drink." "You go first." That got a real grin out of him. He took it back, tipped it up and drank a good third of it. Wiped his mouth on his sleeve. Handed it over. I looked at it for a while. Then I drank. I was braced for it to taste the way that barrel smells. It tasted like nothing. Like the water out of my fridge door. No grit. No pond. No smell. I held the bottle up to the light. What was in the bottle was still brown. What came through the straw was clear. "Well, I'll be." "That's all there is to it." "And it does that with anything?" "Anything fresh. It won't do the ocean, it can't take out salt. But a creek, a pond, a lake, rain water, a stock tank. The tub you filled." "And what's it take out." "There's two stages in there. A membrane that goes down to 0.01 micron. That's what stops bacteria and parasites, the stuff that puts you on the bathroom floor. Then a carbon stage for chemicals and sediment." I stood there holding the bottle. "Warren, where do you even get one." "Same place everybody I work with got theirs. I'll write it down for you." He unscrewed the straw and put it in my hand. "Keep that one. I've got a case. I'll leave you some tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Tell them it's from their mother and she'll sleep better. Leave me out of it. They don't have to believe a word of this. They just have to have it in a drawer on the day." "Warren." "Forget the wood stove if you want. Forget the cash and every other thing I said. I wouldn't. But you could. This one you can't skip." "All right." "When the orders come and everybody's standing in a line for their allotment, the woman with one of these in her purse isn't standing in the water line. There's a word I keep landing on for that. Free. Whatever they shut off, it stops at the edge of that pond down the road for anybody who owns one of these." "Most folks are going to hear about this on the six o'clock news. That's a week too late. You're hearing it from me, today, over a fence. Do something with it." He went back to his wood pile. I went inside. Put it in the junk drawer next to the batteries. Told myself Warren had sat in too many meetings. I left it there two days. Then I sat down with my iPad and started checking up on him. Slovenia really did start rationing gas in March. First country in the EU to do it. The Philippines really did declare a national energy emergency. The head of the International Energy Agency called this "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." In April he went on CNBC and said "We are facing the biggest energy security threat in history." Every single thing Warren said about the oil side checked out. Then I looked up Texas. February 2021. 14.4 million people with their water disrupted. 190 counties. Just like he said. Right down to the man with the eight chickens. Warren left a grocery sack hanging on my back door handle the next morning. Didn't knock. Four more of them inside. I called my daughter that afternoon and said I was coming over. I gave her two. One for her kitchen, one for her husband's truck. I drove to my son's and gave him two. One for the house, one for the diaper bag. The one from the fence stayed in my junk drawer. My son gave me the look. Same one he's been giving me since he was fifteen. Doesn't bother me one bit. If you've had a feeling for a while now that something is off, that the news keeps walking around something without ever saying it, you are not going crazy. The people who deal with this for a living already took care of their own houses. Quietly. No announcement. Warren had one thing dead right. By the time it's on the six o'clock news, the shelf is already bare. The person in the line is the person who heard last. This is the same straw Warren handed me over the fence. I've put the link below. I'm not a prepper. I'm a grandmother with a junk drawer. But when the orders come and the lines start, I'd like to be the woman who took care of it back in September. 👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial EDITED: On September 11th, drones hit that pipeline across Saudi Arabia and shut it down. The one that carries oil around the strait. Warren's side door. I'd written it on the back of an envelope the night he told me. I've still got the envelope. On September 13th, eight ships went through the strait. Eight. It used to be about 85 a day. Another ship got hit that same day. Iran's parliament speaker says it "will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met." AAA said gas jumped 13 cents in a single week. Then last Wednesday my phone rang before 6 in the morning. My sister, out in Wichita. The main water plant there lost power around 5am. It was already running on backup generators because of a storm, and the generators quit. 45 minutes. That's all it was. The pressure dropped and about half a million people, roughly one out of every six people in the state of Kansas, got told to boil their water. Some of the elementary schools closed. The last of it wasn't cleared until Sunday afternoon. She sent me a picture from her Dillons. The water aisle. Bare metal shelves. No war in Kansas. No conservation order. A generator that didn't do its job for 45 minutes. "The tap goes too." He said that to me not three weeks before my own sister was boiling water on the stove to make her coffee. I made this post because I couldn't keep sitting on it. Not after Wichita. Warren still leaves Monday and comes home Thursday. Marlene knows he isn't sick now. He finally sat her down and told her all of it. She says he's at the kitchen table at three most nights. I haven't asked what the meetings are about these days. I don't believe I want to know. My sister ordered a 5-pack from that same kitchen while her water was still on boil. My daughter ordered one too, the night I sent her the Wichita story. My son hasn't ordered a thing. He did leave the one in the diaper bag though. I checked. I went back on the site myself this morning and read every line of the fine print before I told one more person to spend money. Here's what I found. The 5-pack is the one they've got marked most popular, and it comes with a survival guide and 16 emergency checklists thrown in free. Shipping is free. And you get 365 days to change your mind. A full year. "No forms to fill out. No evidence required." Those are their words, I copied them down. So if you've read this far and you're on the fence, you've got a year to decide I'm a silly old woman. I hope I am. 👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial P.S. I finally told my husband. All of it, start to finish. Even the part about the sippy cup. He sat there and didn't say a word the whole time. When I was done he got up, went to the junk drawer, took out the one Warren gave me, walked it out to the garage and put it in the door pocket of his truck. Then he came back in and said two words. "Order more." I already had. P.P.S. If you're wondering how many, here's how I worked it out. One for every person in the house. One for each car, because you won't be home when it happens, you'll be at the grocery or at church. One in the bag by the door. For the two of us that came to five, which is how they sell them anyway. My daughter's house needed five too. If you only get one, fine, get the one. But count heads first. P.P.P.S. Each straw is good for 1,800 gallons. The government's own Ready.gov page says to figure a gallon per person per day. Do that math. That's years, from a creek or a pond or a rain barrel or the tub you filled ahead of time. 0.01 micron membrane plus a carbon stage, so it's bacteria, parasites, sediment and chemicals. No batteries. Nothing to charge. There's no expiry date on them either, the site says they'll keep in a drawer 10 years. Free shipping, and the 365 day money back guarantee I told you about. Warren wouldn't have hung a sack of them on my door and told me to hand them to my grandkids if they didn't work. That was enough for me. P.P.P.P.S. If you're thinking you'll just stack up water in the garage instead, I did that too, and you should. But think about what Warren is doing with that wood pile. Wood burns down. So does stored water. Whatever you've got on those shelves, it's a number that only goes one direction. And when it hits zero the tap isn't safe and the truck isn't coming. The straw is a different kind of thing. As long as there's a pond or a creek or rain coming off a roof somewhere you can walk to, you have water you can drink. One runs out. The other one doesn't. Get the straw. 👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

Texto do anúncio: The man who rented Cabin 6 from me two weeks ago paid for three nights in cash, wrote a first name on my registration card that was not the one on his driver's license, asked me on Wednesday what runs the pump on our well, and on Thursday night, out on my office porch, told me who signs his paycheck. Four days on our place and I never once saw a phone in his hand. Never asked for the WiFi password. Walked down to the creek by himself every evening about sundown and just stood there. I have not told a soul what he said to me that Thursday, not even at church. I'm typing it out now because everything that has been on the news since he left goes right back to that question he asked me about my well. Dale and I have rented out these six cabins for nineteen years. You hand enough strangers a key and you get to where you can size one up before the car door shuts. The fly fisherman who is going to lie about what he caught. The couple up for their anniversary who aren't speaking. The widower who books the same cabin every October and does not want to be asked why. After nineteen years I don't work at it. It just happens. I knew Glenn was something else before he got to my counter. Tuesday, a little before noon. He came up our gravel alone in a plain white sedan and parked at the far end of the lot, not by the office door like everybody does. One bag. A green canvas duffel gone soft at the corners. He stopped in the office doorway before he said a word. Looked at the map of the property I keep on the wall, the one with the cabins and the creek and the road out. Like a man counting doors. Around sixty. Trim. Reading glasses on a cord. Yes ma'am, no ma'am. Didn't ask how the fishing was. Didn't take a brochure for the caverns. Didn't ask where a person gets supper around here. Cash. Three nights. Counted it out in twenties. I ask every guest for a license for the file. The one he slid across said Thomas. The card he filled out said Glenn. I let it lie. Then he took the key, drove down to Cabin 6 and backed that car in behind it so the plate faced the woods. In nineteen years nobody has paid me cash for three nights. Nobody has written down a name that wasn't his while I stood there holding the proof. And nobody has ever come to stay on a fishing creek without a rod. By Wednesday suppertime I had swallowed about six questions I would normally have asked out loud. Thursday night, a quarter to ten. Dale had gone up to the house at eight, he gets up at four-thirty. I was on the office porch folding cabin towels with the screen door propped so I could hear the little TV on the counter. Glenn was in the other rocker on his second beer. He had been there since before dark. Hardly a word. Looking out at where the creek is. You can't see it from there at night. You can only hear it. The news gave Iran about half a minute. Gas up thirteen cents in a week, national average four twenty-seven. One sentence about talks. Then the weather. Glenn listened to it through the screen. Never turned his head. When the weather map came up he said, more to the beer can than to me, "Half a minute. They have got it down to half a minute." I quit folding. I said, "What is that supposed to mean." He took his time. He said, "Nothing. Thinking out loud." I said, "You have been here three days and I bet you haven't said twenty words to me. You've sat on my porch two hours tonight and not asked me one thing about myself, which I promise you is a record for that chair. A man that quiet finally says something, I want to hear the rest of it." He looked right at me for the first time since he checked in. He said, "You watch that every night?" I said, "Every night." He said, "How does it leave you feeling?" I said, "How does it leave me feeling." He said, "The Iran part. Ceasefire. No ceasefire. Paper signed. Strait shut again. What are you left with when it goes to the weather." I had to think about it. I said, "Like I have seen it already. Like it's a rerun. April they had a ceasefire. June President Trump signed that Islamabad paper with Iran's president and three days later the strait was closed again. I quit trying to keep it straight. Last week I got up and started the dishwasher right in the middle of it." He nodded one time. He said, "That is what it's for." I waited. I said, "What what's for." He drank. Set the can on the porch rail. He said, "I ought not to. I don't know you and I don't know who you'd tell. But you caught it when I said it. Mostly people don't. And I have not said any of this out loud to anybody outside my building since March." He looked at the can. He said, "I work for the Energy Department. Emergency planning. I write the long papers on what happens over here if that strait stays shut." He looked up. He said, "I should not have said that. I'd take it kindly if you forgot it." I said, "Glenn." He said, "Yeah." I said, "You paid me cash." He said, "Yeah." I said, "Your license says Thomas." He said, "It does." I said, "You backed your car in so nobody can read the plate from the road." He said, "Yeah." I said, "And yesterday you asked me what runs my well pump." He said, "I know I did." I set the towel down. I said, "What is going on." He looked out at the dark a good while. Then he looked back at me. --- He said, "What they tell you about Iran is true as far as it goes. It just quits halfway. Every night. On purpose." I waited. He said, "The half you get is the cover for the half you don't." I said, "The half I don't being what." He took a drink. He said, "Look how it runs. April, ceasefire. Ten days on, Iran shuts the strait again. May, the Navy starts escorting ships. June, Trump and Pezeshkian sign the memorandum and everybody lets their breath out. Three days. Shut again. July the truce comes apart. August the Navy says it has cleared better than a hundred suspected mines, and that sounds like headway. It is the middle of September and that water is still shut." He looked at me. He said, "You felt it tonight. I watched you. 'It's a rerun.' Now put that in every living room in the country, every night, for six months." A drink. He said, "Folks who notice get tired. Tired folks quit keeping track. Folks who quit keeping track quit asking the one question my office would rather not get asked on camera." He set the can down. I said, "Which is what." He looked at me. He said, "What a closed strait does to your house." I said, "The strait is on every single night." He said, "The strait is on every single night. The map. The little ship pictures. The reporter in the vest. You have heard the word Hormuz more since March than in all your life before it." He looked out at the dark. He said, "What you have not heard, not one time, is what it means for a woman with six cabins and a well if it stays shut through the winter." I waited. He said, "That half never airs. The strait gets the map and the man in the vest. Your kitchen, your daughter's kids' school, the hospital in town, they get nothing." I said, "So what does it do." He took a drink. He said, "A fifth of the oil in the world goes through that water in a normal year. Twenty million barrels a day. The man who runs the International Energy Agency called this the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. On the record, his words. The rich countries drained four hundred million barrels out of their emergency tanks last spring, the most they ever have, and oil is over a hundred dollars anyway. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency in March. Slovenia started rationing gas the day before that, fifty liters a day to a driver. That's Asia and Europe, so you got it for one evening if you got it at all." He looked at me. He said, "It comes here. I could not tell you the week." He took a drink. He said, "Forget gasoline a minute. Think about diesel. Diesel is the truck that carries the treatment chemicals to your town's water plant. Diesel is the backup generator at the pump station. Diesel is the crew that comes out to fix the line. When diesel gets short and gets dear, all the slack goes out. Nothing breaks that day. It's that the next time something does break there is nothing standing behind it." He set the can down. He said, "Watch for the word 'voluntary.' Voluntary conservation. After that, 'advisory.' After that a schedule with your county's name on it. That is the order I would bet on, and I get paid to bet on it." He looked at me. He said, "And here is the piece nobody is going to hand you when it gets here." I waited. He said, "Who goes without has already been written down. I have read it. In January the Department signed an emergency order for Texas. In May it signed another one, for the grid that runs thirteen states and D.C. They spell out how the big data centers get pushed onto their own generators as the last step before the rolling blackouts start. Those orders are public. Nobody read them." He looked at me. He said, "Somebody has already sat down and worked out what order things get switched off in. There is a list. Your kitchen faucet is not on anybody's list. Nobody ever wrote a paper about your well." He let that sit. He said, "So when it comes they will call it a freak thing. A bad week. A once in a lifetime storm. They will call it that the next time too." I didn't say anything for a while. He took a drink. He said, "Tired is what they are after. I've sat in the meetings where my long version gets boiled down to the short one. A tired country does not look underneath anything. By the time your lights flicker you will have been told for a year that it's all nearly settled." I didn't say anything for a long time. --- He took another long drink. He said, "A lot of people in this country figure they are getting ready for something. Canned goods. Silver. Gas cans. Guns, ammunition. A generator from the home center, still in the box." He looked at me. He said, "Nearly every one of them skipped the first thing." I waited. He said, "Water." I said, "Water." He said, "Water." He took a drink. He said, "Nobody on that TV is going to say it. You turn the handle, it comes out. Been that way every day of your life. Mine too. A person can't hardly picture it any other way." He looked at me. He said, "Water is the first thing to go when the power runs short." I waited. He said, "Every treatment plant runs off the power company. Every pump station. Every pump between the river and somebody's sink. And you, you are on a well. Two hundred eighty feet, electric pump, you told me so yourself. The power drops, you've got what's sitting in the pressure tank and that's all you have got." He stopped a second. He said, "Texas. February of 2021. The grid went down in a freeze, and by that Saturday fourteen million people in a hundred and ninety counties had their water fouled up. A hundred and fifty thousand had none at all. Better than two thousand water systems put out boil notices and some of those ran past a month. The head of the state's own environmental agency said it plain. 'My family, my dog, my eight chickens are on day four without water at my house.'" He looked at me. He said, "That was weather. Nobody did that to them. Richmond, Virginia, January of last year. One power outage at the water plant. One. The valves could not close without power, the low rooms took on six feet of water inside ten minutes, and the city and three counties around it boiled their water the better part of a week." He let that sit. He said, "What I write papers about is not one cold snap and it is not one plant." I let that sit too. I said, "We would drive to town and buy water." He said, "You and everybody. Austin, Texas, 2018. Boil notice. The shelves were bare in hours. The grocery chain down there ran better than a hundred trailers of water in one day to catch up, and that was one city with every truck in Texas free to come help. Now picture every city the same week, and the trucks short on diesel." He looked at me. He said, "You have grandkids." It was not a question. He had seen the crayon fish taped up in my office window. I said, "Three. The oldest is eleven." He said, "Some evening about a week into it the littlest one is going to ask you for a drink. And you are going to be standing in your own kitchen with a dry faucet and nothing to hand her." He looked at me. He said, "That is the evening to get ready for. Forget the war and the memorandum and the map with the ships on it. A child and an empty cup. Nobody on TV is going to walk you up to that one ahead of time." I didn't say anything. --- He took another long drink. He said, "The people I work with are fixed for it." I waited. He said, "Two men in my section squared their houses away in March, the week the strait closed. My deputy did hers in June and never said a word. I only know because her husband told my wife at a cookout. There is a retired Army engineer who consults for us and he has been set since the Texas freeze. None of them talk about it at work. None of them are scared either. They have just decided they are not going to be the one standing in that kitchen." He looked at me. He said, "Yesterday. The well." I said, "Yeah." He said, "I was not making conversation. I was checking." I said, "Checking what." He said, "Whether you had ever thought about it. Somebody who has thought about it answers different. They tell you about the hand pump, or the tank, or the spring up the hill. You told me two hundred eighty feet, electric pump, never gave you a day's trouble. Like I'd asked if it looked like rain. So I knew." He set the can down. He said, "Right now you are thinking this is for the bunker crowd. The fellas on cable with the freeze-dried buckets. You are about to tell me you're not a prepper." I was, too. I had my mouth open to say it. He said, "That part works best of all. Long as getting ready looks like something only odd people do, regular people won't do it. Then it comes, and the only ones who were ready are the handful everybody laughed at." He looked at the can. He said, "It all pushes the same direction. The rerun. The being tired. Half a minute and then the weather. It all leaves you sitting still. So when it does come you are sitting right where you were." He took a drink. He said, "Power is the handle. The power goes and the water goes with it. The water goes and you are not running your own house anymore. When the kids drink, when you cook, when you wash, whether the commode flushes, every bit of it waits on whoever decides when the lights come back. You have never had one day without that say-so, so you never noticed you had it." He looked at me. He said, "What you want is something that takes that handle out of their hand ahead of time. Water that comes whether the power does or it doesn't. Something that is in your house this week." He set the can down. He said, "And I do not mean a bunker. I don't mean a pallet of army meals or a generator or a cistern. I mean a tube. About nine inches long. Rides in a coat pocket. Anybody can own one and anybody can work one." He moved the can over. Put his hand flat on his jacket pocket and left it there. --- I said, "A tube." He didn't answer for a bit. He said, "I ought not show you." I said, "You already told me." He looked out at the dark again, where the creek was going by. He said, "Yeah." He took it out of his jacket. Held it in his lap a second. He said, "You keep this to yourself. Dale included. Until you have made up your mind what you are going to do about any of it." I said all right. He set it on the arm of my rocker. A plain tube about nine inches long. I picked it up. More to it than it looked. Solid. I said, "What is it." He said, "A filter." I turned it over. I said, "A filter for what." He said, "Water." I said, "That's all." He said, "That's all." I waited. I could tell he was done volunteering. I said, "How does it work." He looked at his jacket. Then at the tube. He said, "Threads onto a water bottle. Any regular one. The empties in your recycling." I said, "And then." He said, "Then you drink through it. Or you lay down on the bank and drink straight out of the creek with it, if it came to that. Or you hang the bottle upside down and let it drip into a pot." I said, "And what comes out." He said, "Water you can drink." I said, "What's inside it." He looked at me a second. He said, "Two stages in one straw. First a membrane with holes one hundredth of a micron across. Bacteria will not fit through a hole that size. Parasites won't either. Then a carbon stage. The carbon is for chemicals and sediment." I held it up to the porch light like that would tell me something. I said, "Any water." He said, "Any fresh water. Creek. Pond. Rain barrel. A bathtub you filled before the storm got there. Not the ocean. It won't take out salt." I said, "How long is one good for." He said, "Eighteen hundred gallons." I said, "That doesn't mean a thing to me." He said, "The government's own emergency page tells you to figure a gallon a person a day. So call it close to five years for one person." I said, "And then." He said, "Then you get another one. But it does not go bad sitting. No expiration date on it. Leave it in a drawer ten years." I said, "What do you plug it into." He said, "Nothing. No batteries. No pump. You are drinking through a tube." I turned it over again. I said, "This is what the people you work with have." He looked at the dark. He said, "It's what I have. There is one in my daughter's glovebox and she doesn't know it's in there." I waited. I said, "Show me." He looked at me. He said, "Ma'am, I drove nine hours to sit by a creek and not talk to anybody. I did not come here to put on a demonstration." I said, "I want to see it work." He looked at the dark again. Then he got up. Slow, the way you do when your knees have a say. He said, "You got a flashlight." He went down to the creek with my flashlight and the plastic pitcher I make sun tea in. I watched the light bob. He didn't dip from the middle where it runs clear. He went down by the low-water crossing where the neighbor's cows come through, and he came back with a pitcher the color of weak coffee. Bits of leaf in it. Something in there was swimming. He fished an empty water bottle out of my recycling tub, the grocery store kind. Poured the creek water in. You could see the trash floating in it. Threaded the tube onto the top. Tipped the whole thing up over one of my jelly glasses. It came slow. A thin stream. Clear. He held the glass up to the porch light. Clear. Nothing floating. No color to it at all. He handed it to me. I am not going to lie to you. I stood there holding it. He didn't push. I drank it. No taste. No grit. No creek. It tasted like a glass of water at my own sink on any morning of my life. Just water. I looked at the pitcher. Then the glass. Then Glenn. I said, "That is the creek." He said, "Yeah." I said, "From below where the cows cross." He said, "Yes ma'am." Glenn unthreaded the tube and held it out to me. He said, "Keep it." I took it. I walked up to the house at eleven with that tube in my cardigan pocket. I did not sleep. --- Friday morning Dale was at the kitchen table with his coffee and the farm report on. I came in and set the tube down beside his cup. He looked at it. Looked at me. He said, "What's that." I told him. All of it. He said I'd been had. Said a fella drinks two beers on a porch and all of a sudden he's with the government, he has heard that one before. Said I watch too much news and he has been telling me so since spring. I got my boots on and went down to the creek. Same pitcher. Same spot. The cows were standing in it this time. I did the whole thing in front of him. Bottle out of the recycling, brown water in, leaves and all. Tube on top. Tipped it over a jelly glass and set the glass down by his coffee. He looked at me. He looked at the pitcher. He looked at the glass. He drank it. Dale did not say anything for a good minute. For Dale that isn't unusual, but this was a different kind of quiet. He picked up the pitcher and held it to the window. Set it down. Picked up the tube. Turned it over twice. Set it down. Then he said, real low, "He tell you where a person gets these?" --- Glenn pulled out Saturday morning before six. He came up to the office with the one duffel. Paid me cash for the extra night. Asked whether I aimed to do something with what he had told me or just think about it. I told him do. He nodded one time. Put the duffel on the back seat. Went down our gravel slow enough he didn't raise any dust. I haven't heard from him. I don't expect I will. That was nine days ago. In those nine days. Friday, the morning after that porch, drones shut down Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. That is the main way to move oil out overland, around the strait. I only know because I went looking. Sunday a ship was struck in the strait, and the word was the talks with Iran were not starting back up. Eight ships made it through that whole day. Before all this it was eighty-five a day. Wednesday. Wichita, Kansas. About five in the morning the main water plant and pump station lost power. The plant was already running on its backup generators on account of a storm, and the generators quit. It was out about forty-five minutes. The pressure fell, and around half a million people, one out of every six people in Kansas, were told to boil their water. Some grade schools closed. The radio station there ran a picture of the water shelves at a grocery store, empty. The last piece of that system did not get cleared until Sunday afternoon. Forty-five minutes. Friday, Duluth, Minnesota. Power outage, pressure dropped, boil notice. Iran's parliament speaker says the strait "will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met." Three hundred seventy-two ships are sitting out there going nowhere. Oil is a hundred and three dollars. Saturday night I watched all of it get its half a minute and I thought about what he said. It's a rerun. Folks who notice get tired. Tired folks quit keeping track. Folks who quit keeping track quit asking. And I thought about how I answered him about my well. Like he had asked me if it looked like rain. And what that told him about people like me. That tube has been in my purse eleven days. Dale ordered ten of them. Two of the five-packs. One five-pack for our daughter Shelby's house, which is her, Travis and the three kids. The other five are one for my truck, one for his, one for the office drawer, one for the bag in the hall closet that Dale swears is not a go bag, and one for Miss Opal next door, who is eighty-four and on a well the same as us. He did not tell me. I know because the order confirmation came to the cabin email, and because there is a feed store receipt on the refrigerator now with all that written on the back in his block letters. He saw me reading it. He poured himself another cup and went out to the shop. That is how a man changes his mind in this house. He makes a list. --- If you have been watching the news since spring and feeling like it's a rerun, a deal and then no deal, the strait open and then shut, and you've caught yourself getting up to start the dishwasher in the middle of it, I did too. I don't believe anymore that feeling comes from nowhere. Somebody is just fine with you being that tired. They need you worn out. They need you sick of it. They need you looking at that map every night without one person telling you what it does to your own house if the strait stays shut another month. You get the map. You get the ships. You never get the arithmetic. Glenn gave me the arithmetic on my porch that Thursday. The strait shuts off the fuel. Short fuel takes the slack out of the power. No power, no water. And it does not take days. Ask Wichita. It took forty-five minutes. Once there is one simple thing in your kitchen drawer that gets your family clean water with no power at all, that is one thing nobody can switch off on you. Glenn never did say where he got his. Dale ran it down himself that same morning. It is called the Blackout Water Survival Straw, and they sell it off their own website, right here: 👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial They give you 365 days to send it back and get every cent refunded, no forms and no questions. Dale read that part twice hunting for the catch. Shipping is free. I can't tell you how quick it comes because the site does not say, so please don't wait on a storm to order. If you are going to do this, do it before the next half a minute and the weather talks you out of it. You will not be sorry you were the one in your family who had these in a drawer before it mattered. You would be sorry the other way around. 👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial P.S. Yesterday, Sunday, Bloomington, Indiana went under a boil advisory. The water had gone cloudy, nothing to do with Iran and nothing to do with the power. By two or three that afternoon the local paper had the water shelves at the Kroger and the Walmart mostly empty and the downtown Kroger just about cleaned out. The same day. Glenn told me the shelves go in hours. He told me that on a Thursday night. It has been eleven days and I have watched it happen twice, Wichita and Bloomington, and neither one of those was even the thing he is worried about. If he is right about the small ones I am not going to bet my grandkids he's wrong about the big one. P.P.S. I called my sister Connie in Tulsa that first Saturday and told her the whole thing. Connie has been teasing me about my pantry since 1989 and she laughed till she had to set the phone down. Then Wednesday came. Her girl lives in Wichita with two little ones, and she was boiling water on the stove for those babies with the store shelves bare. Connie called me back Thursday and she was not laughing. All she said was, "What was the name of that website." She bought a five-pack for her house and another to carry up to Wichita. That is the way to think about the five-pack. Texto do anúncio: You can survive three weeks without food and three days without water, but you'll shit yourself in 24 hours... and THAT'S the disaster 99% of preppers ignore until it's poisoning their family. I know this because I used to BE one of those 99%. My name's David. And I'm about to tell you something I'm not proud of. But something you NEED to hear before the next storm hits. I thought I had my shit together. Hurricane season, three years ago. I wasn't like my neighbors scrambling at the last minute. I'd been prepping for WEEKS. I had the FEMA checklist printed out. Taped to my garage wall. And I checked every single box: ✓ 72 hours of food for the family ✓ Cases of bottled water ✓ Flashlights, batteries, first aid kit ✓ Battery-powered radio ✓ Even a backup generator My wife made fun of me. "What else could we possibly need?" I remember feeling... proud. Like I was doing the responsible thing. The "dad" thing. Keeping my family safe. Turns out I had no fucking clue. The storm hit on a Tuesday night. Power went out around 2 AM. No big deal. We had the generator. By Wednesday afternoon, the water stopped running. Still no panic. We had bottled water. But then someone tried to flush the toilet. Nothing happened. The tank didn't refill. My daughter looked at me. "Dad... what do we do?" And I realized... I had NO idea. I stood there in that bathroom... Staring at the toilet... And it hit me: We had food. We had water. We had LIGHT. But we had zero plan for what happens AFTER you eat and drink. I went to the garage. Grabbed a 5-gallon bucket. Grabbed a box of trash bags from under the kitchen sink. "We'll make it work," I told my wife. She didn't look convinced. But what choice did we have? I lined the bucket with two bags. Double-bagging. Figured that'd be smart. Put it in the bathroom. Told the kids, "This is our temporary toilet until the water comes back on." My son laughed. My daughter looked mortified. But we didn't have another option. And I thought... it's just a few days, right? Water will come back on. We can handle this. Day three. My daughter woke up with stomach cramps. Food poisoning. Maybe from the canned goods that got too warm in the heat. Maybe from stress. Who knows. What I DO know\... Is that she was in that bathroom... Using that bucket... Every hour. And not just "going." Explosive diarrhea. I'm not trying to be gross here. I'm telling you what happened. Because you need to understand how fast this goes from "manageable inconvenience"... To absolute nightmare. Those trash bags? They weren't made for this. The first one tore. Just... split right down the side. Liquid waste spilled across the bathroom floor. I'm standing there... Gagging... Trying to clean it up with paper towels... While my daughter's crying in the hallway. Humiliated. And my wife's trying to console her... But she's crying too. Because we're ALL realizing... We're in serious trouble. I used two gallons of our stored water... Just trying to clean up that ONE spill. Two gallons. That was supposed to last us for DRINKING. And I just poured it on the bathroom floor. My daughter's still sick. She's going every few hours. I'm changing out bags constantly. Triple-bagging now. But they keep tearing. By day four... The smell is everywhere. It's not contained to the bathroom. It's in the hallway. It's in the air. You can TASTE it. I tried moving the bucket outside. It's 90 degrees. Humid. Flies showed up within an hour. Dozens of them. I tried sealing the bags better. Tying them tighter. But my daughter's still sick. And now my son says his stomach hurts. Not from food poisoning. From touching something. A door handle. The bathroom sink. Who knows. Because the contamination had spread. And I was out of water to clean with. I had to choose: Use our drinking water to wash contaminated surfaces... Or let the contamination spread and hope nobody else gets sick. There's no good answer to that. My wife hasn't slept in two days. I found her standing in the driveway at 3 AM. Just staring at nothing. "I can't be in there anymore," she said. "I just need air that doesn't smell like shit." Day five. I'm sitting in the driveway with her. Dawn's coming up. And I'm looking at my garage. At all those supplies I was so proud of. The cases of water. The boxes of food. The generator humming in the corner. And I realized something that made me want to scream. All that food I stored? It was making things WORSE. Because every meal we ate... Every bottle of water we drank... Had to come out the other end. You can't just INPUT resources into your family... Without dealing with the OUTPUT. And I had NO plan for the output. The better I'd prepped for survival... The worse the sanitation crisis became. My 50 gallons of water? I'd already burned through 12 gallons trying to clean contamination. My two weeks of food? Every meal was another trip to that fucking bucket. Another chance for the bags to fail. Another spill to clean up. The generator I was so proud of? Completely useless. Because you can't power-wash diarrhea. I did everything the "experts" told me to do. I checked every box on FEMA's list. And NONE of them mentioned this. Not once. I tried calling for help on day four. Emergency services. 30-minute hold. When someone finally picked up: "We're prioritizing life-threatening emergencies, sir." I told them my daughter had been sick for three days. That my son might have E. coli from contamination. That we had human waste spreading through our house. "Sir, we recommend boiling water and practicing good hygiene." With what water? With what hygiene supplies? The hospitals were full. The roads were flooded. Nobody was coming. I was completely on my own. With a house that was turning into a biohazard zone. And a family that was getting sicker by the day. A week after we finally got evacuated... After my daughter spent two nights in the hospital getting rehydrated... After we had to hire a hazmat cleaning crew to decontaminate our house... I found a CDC report. About that hurricane. You know what it said? More people died from disease and contaminated water AFTER the storm... Than from the storm itself. Sanitation failure is the #1 cause of death in disaster scenarios. They've known this for DECADES. And nobody puts it on the fucking checklist. Here's what I need you to understand. This isn't about being "grossed out." This isn't about "dealing with an unpleasant smell." This is about contamination. This is about turning your home into a disease vector. This is about your PREP SUPPLIES becoming the weapon that makes your family sick. Because here's the thing nobody tells you: Food and water aren't just survival resources. They're biological inputs. And biological inputs REQUIRE outputs. If you don't have a safe system for handling those outputs... Every meal you stockpiled becomes a liability. Every gallon of water you stored increases the problem. You're not "prepared." You're building a time bomb. And the fuse is already lit. I'm telling you this story for one reason. Because it didn't have to happen. If I'd known... If I'd had the right supplies... If I'd thought about sanitation the same way I thought about food and water... My daughter wouldn't have spent two nights in the hospital. My son wouldn't have gotten sick from contamination. My wife wouldn't have stood in our driveway at 3 AM trying not to cry. We wouldn't have needed a $3,000 hazmat cleaning crew. And I wouldn't be sitting here three years later... Still feeling like I failed my family. All because I didn't have a $20 sanitation kit. What I needed... What EVERY prepper needs... Isn't complicated. You need waste liners that are actually designed to handle human waste. Not regular trash bags. Not "heavy duty" garbage bags. Actual sanitation-grade liners that won't tear or leak. You need absorbent material that turns liquid waste into gel. So it's contained. So it doesn't slosh around. So when you seal the bag, it's actually SEALED. You need an outer disposal bag. So you're not walking around with a single layer between you and contamination. And you need basic hygiene supplies. Toilet paper. Wipes. The stuff you'd normally take for granted. All in one kit. Pre-packaged. Ready to go. So when the power goes out... When the water stops... When your family still needs to eat and drink... You have a SYSTEM. Not a trash bag and hope. After everything my family went through... After I saw how many other families went through the same nightmare... I couldn't just sit on this. So I built what I wish I'd had. The Emergency Sanitation Kit. It's everything you need for emergency bathroom backup. When toilets don't work. When water's not running. When your family still needs to go. Each kit includes: → Heavy-duty waste liner (actually designed for human waste, won't fail like trash bags) → Absorbent material (turns liquid to gel, contains the mess) → Outer disposal bag (double protection, seals everything safely) → Toilet paper + personal wipes Everything stays packed together. Compact enough to store with your other emergency supplies. Ready when you need it. Works with a portable toilet, a bucket, any compatible setup. Right now, we've got a few different options depending on how prepared you want to be: 12 Kits (Starter Supply) - $39.99 Good if you've got a small household or just want to test it out. 24 Kits (Family Supply) - $64.99 (normally $79.98) Enough to cover multiple family members across several days. 36 Kits (Prepared Home) - $84.99 (normally $119.97) ← MOST POPULAR This is what serious preppers are grabbing. Covers your whole household for an extended outage. Complete System (Toilet + 36 Kits) - $119.99 (normally $159.96) You get the portable folding toilet PLUS 36 sanitation kits. The full setup so you're not scrambling for a bucket. Look. I hope you never need this. I hope your power never goes out for more than a few hours. I hope your toilets always flush. But hope isn't a plan. And I learned that lesson the hard way. Watching my daughter cry in the hallway. Watching my wife break down in the driveway. Spending two nights wondering if my daughter was going to be okay. Writing a $3,000 check to clean contamination out of my house. You don't want to learn it that way. Because here's the thing: You've already done the hard work. You've stockpiled food. You've stored water. You've bought the flashlights and batteries. You're ONE piece away from actually being prepared. And depending on which package you choose... That piece costs anywhere from $40 to $120. Less than a weekend grocery run. Right now, we've got these in stock. But I'm looking at inventory... And we're down to 18 kits left from this shipment. I'm not trying to create fake urgency here. I'm telling you what I'm looking at. And based on how fast these have been moving... Especially with hurricane season... I'd be surprised if we have any left by this weekend. So if you're serious about closing that gap in your prep... And you want to make sure your family has what mine didn't... I'd grab yours now. And look... If you get this and decide it's not for you... We have a 30-day money-back guarantee. No questions asked. I'd rather have you TRY this... And decide you don't need it... Than have you caught in a situation like I was... Without it. Because I promise you... When your toilet stops working... And your daughter's sick... And you're standing in your bathroom with a torn trash bag leaking across the floor... You will think about this moment. And you will wish you'd grabbed the kit when you had the chance. Don't be me three years ago. Be smarter than I was. Click the link below. Choose the package that makes sense for your family. And make sure you grab yours before we're out of stock. Because the next storm doesn't care if you're ready. But your family will. ⇒ Get Your Emergency Sanitation Kit (Only 18 left): https://thestandbysupply.com/products/emergency-sanitation-kit?pb=0 Stay prepared, David P.S. Remember... food and water are only PART of the equation. If you can't safely handle what comes OUT... You're not prepared. You're just stocked up. There's a difference. And that difference could save your family from what mine went through. ⇒ Don't wait. Choose your package here: https://thestandbysupply.com/products/emergency-sanitation-kit?pb=0
