Texto do anúncio: My neighbour's husband came back from a work trip to Whitehall last month and started quietly shutting his family's life down. Sold the narrowboat he spent six years doing up. Cancelled the Norwegian fjords cruise for their 35th anniversary. Took cash out of the bank. A lot of it. Talked his son into bringing the grandkids back from Spain. His wife was sure a consultant had given him bad news and he was keeping it from her. He told me the real reason over our back fence, and it came down to one word. That was five weeks ago. I still haven't told my husband. But I've quietly done every single thing he told me to do, before the rest of this road works it out. His name is Graham. 61 years old. Thirty-four years in the electricity networks. Control rooms, mostly. The steadiest man I know. I've lived next door to Graham and Linda for 14 years. Our grandkids run through the same sprinkler. Graham goes Monday and comes back Thursday. Warrington mostly. This year, a lot of London. Whitehall. Doesn't say much. Waves from the mower. You ask him something, you get the answer and nothing extra. In 14 years I have not once seen that man rattled. So when he started acting odd in August, I noticed. First it was the boat. Then the cruise. Linda had that brochure stuck on her fridge since Christmas. Then the bank. She found the withdrawal slips in his jacket pocket. Then a van pulled up from Stansted. Their son Daniel, his wife, two little girls and the dog. Into the spare rooms "for a while." Nobody would tell her why. Then the deliveries started. Plain brown boxes. A whole pallet one time. Straight into his shed with the door pulled to behind him. Linda sat at my kitchen table on a Wednesday and cried. "He's ill. I know he's ill. He's had some kind of news and he's putting his affairs in order and he won't tell me." I didn't know what to say to her. Then Saturday morning I was at the sink, looked out of my kitchen window, and saw Graham doing something I have never seen him do in 14 years. He was splitting logs. Two tonnes at least, tipped beside his shed. Graham out there in his old jumper with a maul, swinging. Graham and Linda have a gas fire. They've had a gas fire since the day they moved in. He'd been at it the best part of an hour. No radio. No gloves. Just swinging. I stood there and watched him a good 20 minutes. Then I made two teas and walked out to the fence. "Graham." He stopped. "Brought you a tea." He looked at the maul. Looked at the pile. Looked at me. Then he leaned the maul on the chopping block and came over. "Thank you." "Graham, what on earth are you doing?" "Getting some logs in." "Logs." "Yep." "For the gas fire." "Log burner's being fitted Thursday." I laughed. He didn't. "Graham. Come on now." "It's a stove. People have stoves. It's no big thing." "A box of candles is no big thing. You've got a timber yard back there." I nearly got a smile out of him. "Linda thinks I've lost the plot." "Linda thinks you're dying. She sat at my table on Wednesday and cried about it." That one got to him. He looked down into his mug. "I know. She asked me straight out that night." "She thinks you've got six months and you won't tell her, Graham." "I know." "So what is it really." Nothing. He drank some tea. Looked off past his shed at the trees at the bottom of the gardens. I waited. "You know I can't talk about work." "I didn't ask about work." "Anything I've got to say right now is work." I kept my mouth shut. "I've sat in a lot of rooms since the spring. That's all it is." "All right." "A few of them I'd have paid good money not to be in." I came at it another way. "Graham. What are you getting ready for?" That one he felt. He let out a long breath. "You been following the oil thing? The strait?" "Hormuz. Course. Petrol's daft money again. It's all anybody talks about in the queue at the Co-op." He nodded slowly. "That's the bit you're allowed to watch." "Meaning what." "Meaning the news shows you the ships. The rooms I've been in aren't about ships. They're about what gets done here, at home, once things get tight enough. None of that's been on your telly." "What gets done." He went quiet again. Then: "You remember 2020?" "Which part." "The part where somebody decided which shops were essential. Where they told you how many people could sit round your own table at Christmas. Where three weeks turned into a year." "I remember." "Well, they kept the binder. All of that got built once and nobody took it apart." I went cold right down both arms. "Kept it for what." "For this. Same binder. New reason." "Graham." "Fuel goes first. They won't call it rationing. Hospitals, emergency services, food lorries first. You and me get what's left and a queue to stand in." "That doesn't happen here." "It did happen here. The three-day week. You and I are both old enough to remember our mums doing tea by candlelight. And 2021, when the forecourts ran dry and they had the army driving the tankers. And it's happening right now. The government's own National Security Strategy says we have to 'actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario.' Their words, not mine. We're not at the front of the queue. But we're in it." "Okay." "Then the lorries. Diesel goes where they say it goes. Shelves get thin, then patchy." "Okay." "Then the power. They've got a word for it. Rota disconnections. Your postcode goes off for three hours, then the next one does. Kindly don't put the kettle on between four and seven." "Graham." "And 2020 had an end because a virus runs its course. This one runs until the ships move. They've been attacking tankers in and around that strait since the start of the year. The Royal Navy's lot keep putting out warnings. There was a ship hit sixteen miles off Oman in September. The interim deal in June left the traffic well below normal and it's still well below normal. A fifth of the world's oil goes through that water in an ordinary year. Nobody in those rooms is talking in weeks." I just stood there. "That's why Daniel and the girls are in my spare rooms. That's why the boat's gone. That's why there's a stove coming Thursday." "All right. So what do I do?" He looked at me a while. Then he sort of laughed. A worn out laugh. "Tell you the truth, everything I just listed is the easy part." "Easy?" "It's what your nan would've done without anybody telling her. Anybody who lived through the three-day week. None of it takes inside knowledge. It's chores." "You sold a boat you loved, Graham. Don't stand there and tell me that's chores." "It is to the people who know." I didn't answer him. "None of that is what has me up at three in the morning." "Then what does." Long drink of tea. "Something that came up about a month in. One slide, in a room I only got into because somebody was off sick. They spent four minutes on it and moved on. I'd give up every box in that shed before I'd give up my answer to it." "Your answer to what?" He looked right at me. "The radio." "The radio?" "When this gets bad, knowing what's going on is the whole game. Ahead of cash. Ahead of a full tank. Ahead of that log pile." "The radio." "You can be cold a good while. You can get through a dark house with candles. But the day the phones go, you're on your own. And you won't even know how on your own you are. You won't know if it's your street or the whole country. You won't know if your daughter's all right. You won't know where to go or when it's coming back." "Go how." "Spain and Portugal. 28th of April last year. The whole grid went, both countries. Tens of millions of people. No trains, no metro, no traffic lights, no cash machines, no phones, no internet. Card payments didn't work. The mobiles stopped and nobody had any information. Some places were sixteen hours with no power. The ones who knew it was the whole country and not just their road were the ones sat next to a battery radio." "But we've got our mobiles." "The phones go too. Nobody ever sees that one coming." "Graham." "Your mobile works because the mast at the end of the road has power. Mast loses power, it runs on its backup for a few hours if you're lucky. Then nothing. Your landline? They've switched you to digital. It goes through the router. The router's on the mains. Ofcom says the battery backup only has to last 'at least one hour.' And the old copper line, the one that worked in a power cut, gets switched off on the 31st of January. It's on gov.uk. Look it up." "Storm Arwen, November 2021. Over a million homes lost power. Nearly four thousand were off for more than a week. Up in Aberdeenshire and Northumberland the masts went with the power. No landline, no mobile, no leccy. People sat in freezing houses for days not knowing when anybody was coming." "A week." "Over a week. From one storm. Storm Éowyn, January last year, 285,000 homes and businesses in Northern Ireland, and NIE told some of them they could be waiting till the 3rd of February. Berlin, this January. Somebody set fire to the power cables. Five days, in the freezing cold, about a hundred thousand people. Czech Republic, the summer before last, half a million off and about a thousand mobile masts running on backup. Heathrow, one fire at one substation, and the busiest airport in Europe shut for the day." "Every one of those was one place at a time. With the rest of the country standing by to send help." "What I'm telling you about is everywhere at once. And nobody's standing by, because everybody's in it." He set his mug on the fence post. "Picture it. Day three. Your grandkids are frightened. It's pitch dark at half four. The phone says No Service. The telly's off, the internet's off. Your daughter's on the other side of town and you don't know if she's all right, and she doesn't know if you are. And you're stood in your kitchen with a candle trying to work out if it's your road or the whole of Britain." "Don't." "I know. I'm sorry. But that's the one that gets me up at night. Everybody's staring at the petrol pump. Nobody's looking at the phone in their hand." "This can't be right." "Ask yourself why every headline says oil and not one of them says phones. The Department of Health put it on gov.uk in black and white. In a national power outage, phone, internet and television services would be disrupted, so emergency communications to the public would be limited to radio. BBC Radio 2 and Radio 4. That's it. Now walk down this road and count how many houses have a radio that works without the mains. They won't say it out loud, because the minute they do, there won't be a wind-up radio left in the country by teatime. That's what 'avoiding a panic' means." "All right. So what are you doing about it?" He looked at his mug. "We're sorted." "What's that mean." "Means we're sorted." "Graham." "I'd rather leave it there." "You haven't left one thing there in twenty minutes." Nothing. "Graham. You've just stood my granddaughter in my kitchen in the pitch dark. You do not get to say that to me and go back to chopping logs." He looked at me a long moment. "It's not something I'm meant to be passing round." "Passing what round." "What people in my line of work are doing at their own houses." "Tell me." He sighed. Looked at the shed. Looked at the logs. Looked back at me. "There's an item. One particular item. Everybody I trust in this business has them. The chap who runs our control room up north. A woman on my team who did twenty years in the Royal Navy before she came to us. My boss ordered ten back in the spring, for his kids and the caravan, when all anybody else was buying was jerry cans." "What item." "It's small. It's cheap, considering. It's no secret, you could look it up tonight. It's just that nobody outside my little world has tied it to any of this yet." "Graham. What is it." One more long look. Then: "Stay there." He went in his shed. Came back out with something in his hand. Red. About the size of a mobile phone. A black handle folded flat on the back. A silver aerial. He held it up. "This." "A radio?" "An emergency radio. AM and FM. You wind it with that crank, or you leave it on the windowsill and the little solar panel on top does it, or you plug it into USB-C while the power's still on. Torch on the end. SOS alarm. And a 2000 mAh battery inside it that'll put charge back into your phone. No socket. No batteries to go flat in a drawer." "And that's what..." "That's what we've all got. There's one in Linda's glovebox, she just doesn't know what it is. One in each of the girls' rucksacks. That's the item." "That little thing." "That's why it works. Goes in a handbag. Needs no mains and no batteries. And nobody can switch it off." "Graham, does that thing actually work?" "I'll let you answer that yourself in about five minutes. Go and get your phone." I went and got it. Nine per cent, because it's always nine per cent. Followed him round the back of his house. He opened the cupboard under his stairs where the fuse box is. Flicked the main switch. The whole house went. The fridge stopped humming. The router light by the telly went out. Somewhere upstairs Daniel shouted "Dad!" He took my phone off me. Turned the Wi-Fi on. Nothing to connect to. One bar, the way it always is in that hallway. Then he put the radio in my hand. "Wind it." "Graham." "Wind it." "You go first." That got a real grin out of him. He took it back, turned the crank a good few times and handed it back. I clicked it on. Pushed it to FM. Turned the dial. I was braced for hiss. It was Radio 4. Clear as anything. A man reading the shipping forecast in a house with no electricity. "Well, I'll be." "That's all there is to it." He pressed the button on the end. The torch lit the whole hallway, right up the stairs. Then he took the cable out of his pocket, plugged my phone into the side of the radio, and the little charging symbol came up on my screen. Then he pressed the SOS. It nearly took my ears off. Linda shouted something from the garden I won't repeat. "And it does that with no power at all?" "No power at all. Crank, sun, or the battery inside. Whatever the grid's doing." "And what's it pick up." "AM and FM. The BBC keeps FM going when everything else goes. That's the whole point of FM. It works almost everywhere." I stood there holding it in the dark. "Graham, where do you even get one." "Same place everybody I work with got theirs. I'll write it down for you." He flicked the power back on. The fridge started up again. He put the radio in my hand. "Keep that one. I've got a box of them. I'll leave you some tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Tell them it's from their mother and she'll sleep better. Leave me out of it. They don't have to believe a word of this. They just have to have it in a drawer on the day." "Graham." "Forget the log burner if you want. Forget the cash and every other thing I said. I wouldn't. But you could. This one you can't skip." "All right." "When the lights go and everybody on this road is sat in the dark refreshing a phone with no signal, the woman with one of these on her windowsill knows what's going on. There's a word I keep landing on for that. Free. Whatever they switch off, it stops at the edge of that radio." "Most folk are going to hear about all this on the six o'clock news. That's a week too late, and it's assuming the telly's working. You're hearing it from me, today, over a fence. Do something with it." He went back to his log pile. I went inside. Put it in the kitchen drawer next to the batteries. Told myself Graham had sat in too many meetings. I left it there two days. Then I sat down with my iPad and started checking up on him. The National Security Strategy really does say we must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario." June 2025. It names Russia, Iran, China and North Korea. The National Risk Register 2026 really does have a national power outage on it. Rated catastrophic. "All consumers without backup generators would lose their mains electricity supply instantaneously and without warning." Instantaneously. And without warning. The Department of Health really did write that emergency communications would be limited to radio. Radio 2 and Radio 4. "The most power resilient form of communication." The copper landline really does get switched off on the 31st of January 2027. And the government's own Be Ready checklist, the one they want every household to have, really does say "FM radio (battery / wind up)." Right there between the torch and the power bank. Every single thing Graham said checked out. Then I looked up Storm Arwen. Over a million customers. Nearly four thousand off for over a week. Just like he said. Graham left a carrier bag hanging on my back door handle the next morning. Didn't knock. Four more of them inside. I rang my daughter that afternoon and said I was coming over. I gave her two. One for her kitchen, one for her husband's van. She said, "Mum, I'm not a prepper." I said neither am I, love. I drove to my son's and gave him two. One for the house, one for the changing bag. The one from the fence stayed in my kitchen drawer. My son gave me the look. Same one he's been giving me since he was fifteen. Doesn't bother me one bit. If you've had a feeling for a while now that something is off, that the news keeps walking round something without ever saying it, you are not going mad. The people who deal with this for a living have already sorted their own houses. Quietly. No announcement. Graham had one thing dead right. By the time it's on the six o'clock news, the shelf is already bare. The person sat in the dark is the person who heard last. This is the same radio Graham handed me over the fence. I've put the link below. I'm not a prepper. I'm a nan with a kitchen drawer. But when the lights go and the phones go with them, I'd like to be the woman who sorted it back in October. 👉 https://helorafit.com/pages/uk-emergency-radio-report EDITED: Then the storms came. Austen, and straight after it Boelo, from the 23rd to the 25th of October. Power cuts hit 838,700 homes across Britain. By seven o'clock on the Sunday night, 90,600 were still without power. Two people died. I'd written Graham's list on the back of an envelope the night he told me. I've still got the envelope. My sister's road was one of the 838,700. She rang me the next day, once she could. Her mobile went to No Service about four hours in. Her landline went the second the router did, because they'd switched her to digital in the summer and nobody told her what that meant. She sat in the dark with a candle and no idea whether it was her village or half the country. She said the worst bit wasn't the cold. It was not knowing. "The phones go too." He said that to me not three weeks before my own sister was sat in her kitchen in the dark with a phone that said No Service. Diesel tanks at the FM transmitter towers to keep the generators going for three days. And one line I copied down word for word: "Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack." The same piece said the copper landline, the one that "would work even in a power cut," goes on the 31st of January. I made this post because I couldn't keep sitting on it. Not after my sister. Texto do anúncio: The last thing your family will hear before the grid fails is nothing. No warning. No siren. No announcement. Just the moment the lights go out and every device in the house goes quiet at the same second. I know this because I maintain the civilian grid. I have maintained it for 26 years. And the UK's National Security Strategy, published on 24 June 2025, said that for the first time in many years Britain must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario". They are not worried about the dark. They are worried about the silence that comes after it. My name is Gareth. I am 52. Master electrician. Twenty-six years with a regional utility in the Midlands. I do not read about the grid. I open the panels. I test the load. I file quarterly condition assessments. And I need to tell you something about those assessments that the government's own papers now say in plain English , not about power. About what you lose when the power stops. Most people think a grid failure means the lights go out. That is the first thing that happens. It is not the dangerous thing. The dangerous thing is what goes dark in the hours after the lights , the things you did not know were connected to the same system. Your phone connects to a mobile mast. That mast runs on the grid. The government's Be Ready pages say your mobile might stop working if your local mast is in the affected area. In the most serious circumstances your mobile, landline and broadband could all be down. Every phone in your house. Every phone on your street. Every phone in your town. Quiet at the same hour. Your television connects through a box connected to a router connected to the wall. Same grid. Same failure. Same hour. gov.uk Be Ready says that in a power cut your TV or internet might not be working. Your laptop connects through the same router. Same grid. Same silence. Your kid's tablet. Your wife's watch. The doorbell camera. The baby monitor. The smart speaker your daughter asks questions to before bed. Every single thing in your house that connects your family to the outside world runs through the same grid the National Risk Register 2026 calls a "Catastrophic" national power outage: "All consumers without backup generators would lose their mains electricity supply instantaneously and without warning." I have been filing this in my reports for years. Not the technical language , the human language. I write about cascade failures and single-point vulnerabilities and fuel-chain dependencies. But what I am actually writing about is silence. Every report I have filed for 26 years is a description of how fast your family loses contact with the outside world when the system I maintain stops working. The Department of Health and Social Care put the human part in writing on 16 December 2025. In a national power outage, "phone, internet and television services would be disrupted." For that reason, "emergency communications to the public would be limited to radio (BBC Radio 2 and Radio 4), which is the most power resilient form of communication." Radio. Because the people who wrote that understand what most families do not , the most dangerous thing about a grid failure is not what stops working. It is what stops talking. I told my wife on a Wednesday. Not about transformers. Not about substations. I sat across from her at the kitchen table and I said: "Helen, I need to tell you something about the house." "What about the house?" "Everything in this house that tells you what is happening outside , the phone, the TV, the laptop, the tablet , all of it connects through the same grid. The grid I maintain. When the grid fails, you lose all of it. Not as a rumour. The National Risk Register says the loss is instantaneous and without warning. About 60% of demand reconnected within 2 days. Beyond 7 days they expect full and stable power restored to all of Great Britain. Until then you are sitting in this kitchen with the kids and you do not know if there is a flood warning or an evacuation order or a chemical spill south of Coventry. You do not know if the schools are closed. You do not know if the motorway is open. You do not know anything. Because every way you find things out runs through the same system that just died." She looked at her phone on the counter. I have seen that look before. I saw it on my mum's face. On my neighbour's face. The look of someone seeing a permanent thing as temporary for the first time. The phone sits on the counter like a fixture. Like a tap. Like a light switch. It is not a fixture. It is rented , from a mast, from a grid, from a fuel tanker, from a strait. "So how do I know what is happening?" "Right now you do not." She sat with that for a long time. Then she said something that stayed with me for days. "So the person who is supposed to warn me about the emergency , is already gone before the emergency starts?" Yes. That is exactly what those documents describe. The warning path dies before the warning is needed. The grid fails. The masts and the broadband fail with it. Spain and Portugal, on 28 April 2025, showed the shape of it: the most severe blackout on the European power system in over 20 years, tens of millions without trains, metros, traffic lights, ATMs, phone connections and internet. BBC reported that mobile phones had stopped working and nobody had any information. By the time your family needs information to make a decision , stay or leave, shelter or move, which roads, which direction , the only devices that could deliver that information are already dead. Aber Michael, der stille Michael, der mit seiner Frau immer weiter hinten sitzt und nie groß auffällt, ist einfach zu seinem Auto gegangen und weggefahren. Nicht so gestresst, wie ich es bei jemandem in ihrer Lage erwartet hätte. „Julia, wie kommt ihr zurecht?“, habe ich gefragt. „Ich hab das mit dem Wasser gehört. Und ihr habt keinen Strom?“ Sie hat gelächelt. „Uns geht's eigentlich richtig gut. Michael war am Sonntagmittag bei uns.“ „Michael? Aus der Gemeinde?“ „Ja. Er stand vielleicht zwanzig Minuten nach dem Gottesdienst vor unserer Tür. Er hat geklopft, mit so einem kleinen blauen Ding in der Hand, und gesagt: ‚Ich hab von dem Abkochgebot gehört. Darf ich euch was zeigen?‘“ Julia hat mir die ganze Geschichte direkt da zwischen den Müsliregalen erzählt, und ehrlich gesagt hat das verändert, wie ich darüber denke, was es heißt, Menschen zu helfen. „Am Sonntagmorgen waren wir komplett im Panikmodus“, hat sie gesagt. „Um 8 Uhr kam die Warnung zum Abkochgebot aufs Handy. Mit drei Kindern unter sieben und mir im siebten Monat ist bei uns das Wasser ruckzuck weg.“ „Und ihr konntet das Leitungswasser nicht abkochen, weil ihr keinen Strom hattet?“ „Genau. Das Unwetter hat Samstagnacht in unserer ganzen Straße den Strom lahmgelegt. Und dann noch das Abkochgebot. Da stand drin, dass das Wasserwerk E.-coli-Bakterien im Trinkwasser gefunden hat und alle das Wasser abkochen sollen, bevor sie es trinken, Essen damit zubereiten oder sich auch nur die Zähne putzen.“ Sie hat ihren Einkaufswagen ein Stück zur Seite geschoben. „Aber ohne Strom konnten wir nichts abkochen. Unser Herd ist elektrisch. Wir haben keinen Gasgrill und keinen Campingkocher. Wir saßen komplett fest.“ „Und was habt ihr gemacht?“ „Daniel, mein Mann, ist rumgefahren und hat an allen möglichen Tankstellen nach Wasser in Flaschen gesucht. Aber im Umkreis von 15 Kilometern war das Wasser überall schon ausverkauft. Die Leute hatten gehamstert, seit das Abkochgebot raus war. An einer Tankstelle hieß es, die nächste Lieferung kommt frühestens am Mittwoch.“ „Am Sonntagmittag war ich kurz davor durchzudrehen. Wir haben das bisschen Flaschenwasser, das noch übrig war, eingeteilt. Die Kinder wollten ständig was trinken, und ich musste ihnen immer wieder sagen: ‚Nur einen Schluck‘ oder ‚Wartet noch ein bisschen‘. Ich war gestresst, fix und fertig und hatte panische Angst, dass uns das Wasser komplett ausgeht.“ Sie hat kurz innegehalten. „Und genau da hat Michael an die Tür geklopft.“ „Was hat er gesagt, als ihr aufgemacht habt?“, habe ich gefragt. „Er war total ruhig. Er hat gesagt: ‚Hey, ich hab von dem Abkochgebot gehört und dass ihr, genau wie wir, keinen Strom habt. Ich hab ein bisschen Notfallausrüstung im Auto. Darf ich euch was zeigen, das vielleicht hilft?‘“ „Wir haben ihn reingebeten, und er hat diesen kleinen blauen Wasserfilter aus seinem Notfallrucksack geholt. Der sah so simpel aus, ungefähr so groß wie ein Zahnbürstenetui für die Reise. Ich weiß noch, wie ich dachte: So was Kleines kann uns doch niemals helfen.“ „Aber Michael hat gesagt: ‚Das ist ein Wasserfilter in Militärqualität. Der filtert Bakterien raus und Parasiten, die Keime, die Wasser gefährlich machen. Man braucht keinen Strom. Einfach filtern und trinken.‘“ „Und, hast du ihm geglaubt?“ „Erst mal nicht. Ich meine, das klang zu schön, um wahr zu sein. Wir haben E. coli im Trinkwasser, und dieses kleine Röhrchen soll das lösen?“ Julia hat gelächelt. „Aber dann ist Michael raus in unseren Garten gegangen, hat eine Wasserflasche direkt aus einer Pfütze gefüllt, diesen Filter auf die Flasche geschraubt und daraus getrunken. Direkt vor unseren Augen.“ „Das hat er getrunken?“ „Er hat gesagt: ‚Ich benutze solche Filter seit fünf Jahren. Auf Missionseinsätzen, beim Camping, bei Stromausfällen. Ich bin kein einziges Mal krank geworden. Die Hohlfasermembran filtert bis auf 0,1 Mikron. E.-coli-Bakterien sind 2 Mikron groß. Die kommen rein physisch nicht durch.‘“ Sie hat sich auf ihren Einkaufswagen gestützt. „Dann hat er noch eine Flasche gefüllt, sie Daniel in die Hand gedrückt und gesagt: ‚Probier mal. Überzeug dich selbst.‘ Das hat Daniel dann auch gemacht. Er meinte, es schmeckt wie ganz normales Leitungswasser. Dann hat Michael eine für mich gefüllt. Dann eine für unsere Älteste, Sofia.“ „Wir haben alle gefiltertes Wasser aus unserem eigenen Hahn getrunken, trotz Abkochgebot. Und es war völlig in Ordnung. Normal. Sauber.“ „Wie lange hat das alles gedauert?“ „Vielleicht fünf Minuten. Das haut mich immer noch um. Während alle anderen auf dem Parkplatz noch darüber geredet haben, wie man Hilfe organisiert, war Michael schon zu uns gefahren und hatte unser Problem gelöst. In fünf Minuten.“ „Darf ich was fragen?“, habe ich gesagt. „Ich verstehe das mit dem Abkochgebot immer noch nicht ganz. Warum konntet ihr das Leitungswasser gar nicht benutzen?“ Julia hat genickt. „Ich hab das auch erst richtig verstanden, als Michael es erklärt hat.“ „Er hat gesagt, wenn ein Wasserwerk eine Verunreinigung feststellt, so wie bei uns E. coli, dann heißt das, dass das Wasser nicht richtig aufbereitet wird, bevor es in den Häusern ankommt. Entweder hatte das Wasserwerk bei dem Unwetter keinen Strom, oder die Filteranlagen sind ausgefallen, oder irgendwas anderes ist schiefgelaufen.“ „Abkochen macht die Bakterien unschädlich, dann ist das Wasser wieder sicher. Aber wenn der Strom weg ist, so wie bei uns, kannst du nichts abkochen. Dann kommt zwar Wasser aus deinem Hahn, aber du kannst es nicht benutzen.“ Sie hat mich ernst angesehen. „Michael hat gesagt, so was passiert ständig. Bei jedem Hochwasser, bei jedem schweren Unwetter, bei jedem Ausfall in der Infrastruktur fallen Wasserwerke aus, und plötzlich haben ganze Städte kein sicheres Trinkwasser mehr. Das Ahrtal nach der Flut, manche Orte monatelang. Passau beim Hochwasser 2013. Und elf Jahre später in Passau gleich noch mal.“ „Das Wasser hört nicht sofort auf zu fließen. Aber es ist nicht sicher. Und wenn das Wasserwerk lange genug ausfällt, sinkt irgendwann der Druck, und es kommt gar kein Wasser mehr.“ „So oder so hast du ein Problem. Entweder hast du verunreinigtes Wasser, das du nicht trinken kannst, oder du hast gar kein Wasser.“ „Aber mit dem Filter …“ „Mit dem Filter war das egal. Aus verunreinigtem Leitungswasser wurde sofort Trinkwasser, aus dem Bakterien und Parasiten rausgefiltert sind. Kein Strom nötig. Kein Abkochen. Kein Warten. Einfach filtern und trinken.“ „Hat Michael noch was gesagt?“, habe ich gefragt. „Bevor er gegangen ist?“ Julias Blick hat sich verändert. Wurde nachdenklicher. „Ja. Er hat etwas gesagt, das mir echt hängen geblieben ist. Etwas, an das ich seitdem ständig denken muss.“ Sie hat den Einkaufswagen losgelassen. „Er hat gesagt: ‚Echte Nächstenliebe heißt nicht, Hilfe zu organisieren. Sondern vorbereitet zu sein, damit du in dem Moment helfen kannst, in dem du, deine Familie oder dein Nachbar Hilfe braucht.‘“ „Wie hat er das gemeint?“ „Er hat erklärt, dass viele Christen in Krisen helfen wollen. Das wollen sie wirklich. Aber wenn dann tatsächlich eine Krise kommt, sind sie nicht bereit.“ „Wie viele Familien schon schlimme Krisen durchmachen mussten, während …“ Sie hat mich angesehen. „Michael hat gesagt: ‚Ich hab diese Filter im Auto, im Haus, im Notfallrucksack. Nicht, weil ich paranoid bin. Sondern weil ich weiß, dass Infrastruktur manchmal ausfällt. Und wenn das passiert, müssen wir vorgesorgt haben, damit wir nicht leiden müssen.‘“ „Er hat auch gesagt: ‚Wenn du nicht vorbereitet bist, kannst du niemandem helfen. Nicht deiner Familie, nicht deinen Kindern, nicht deinen Nachbarn. Dann bist du nur einer mehr, der selbst Hilfe braucht. Einer mehr, der im Laden um die paar Flaschen Wasser kämpft, die es noch gibt.‘“ Julia hat ihr Handy rausgeholt und mir eine Nachricht gezeigt, die Michael ihr am selben Abend noch geschickt hatte. Es war ein Bibelvers. Sprüche 21,5. „Die Bestrebungen des Fleißigen bringen nur Gewinn; wer sich aber überstürzt, hat nur Schaden davon.“ Darunter hatte Michael geschrieben: „Vorsorge ist Fleiß. Es heißt, vorauszuplanen, damit du für andere sorgen kannst, wenn sie dich brauchen.“ „Hat Michael euch den Filter dagelassen?“, habe ich gefragt. „Hat er“, hat Julia gesagt. „Wir haben auch noch welche für den Rest der Familie bestellt …“ „Er hat uns die Website gegeben, wo er sie bestellt. Virest. Er hat gesagt, er benutzt die schon eine ganze Weile und hat immer ein paar mehr da, extra damit er sie in Notfällen an Leute weitergeben kann.“ „Er wollte nicht mal auf einen Kaffee bleiben. Hat nur gesagt: ‚Ruft an, wenn ihr noch was braucht‘, und ist wieder gefahren. Daniel wollte ihm Geld geben, ihm seine Zeit bezahlen, seine Hilfe. Michael hat abgelehnt. Er hat gesagt: ‚So handelt Christus. Wir kümmern uns umeinander.‘“ Julia hatte ein bisschen Tränen in den Augen. Ich stand da im Supermarkt und habe an den Sonntag gedacht. So sieht Nächstenliebe wirklich aus. Nicht organisieren. Nicht diskutieren. Nicht planen. Machen. Und das kannst du nur, wenn du vorher vorgesorgt hast. Am Sonntag darauf habe ich Michael nach dem Gottesdienst gesehen. Hab ihn auf dem Parkplatz erwischt, als er mit seiner Frau zu seinem Auto ging. „Michael, Julia hat mir erzählt, was du letzte Woche für sie getan hast.“ Er hat gelächelt. „Wie geht's ihnen?“ „Super. Montagabend war der Strom wieder da. Aber sie hat gesagt, schon vorher ging's ihnen gut, dank dem Filter, den du ihnen gezeigt hast.“ Er hat genickt. Hat kein großes Ding draus gemacht. „Darf ich dich was fragen?“, habe ich gesagt. „Warum hast du diese Filter im Auto? Wie lange machst du das schon?“ Er hat sich an sein Auto gelehnt. „Jetzt ungefähr fünf Jahre. Angefangen hab ich nach einem Missionseinsatz in Mittelamerika. Wir mussten dort Wasser aus Flüssen filtern, weil man sich auf die Versorgung vor Ort nicht verlassen konnte. Da hab ich gesehen, dass so etwas Einfaches für Familien einen riesigen Unterschied machen kann.“ „Als ich zurück war, hab ich angefangen, immer Filter im Auto, im Haus und im Notfallrucksack zu haben. Nicht, weil ich ein Prepper bin oder mir Sorgen wegen der Endzeit mache. Sondern weil Infrastruktur ausfällt. Nicht jeden Tag, aber oft genug.“ „Stromausfälle. Sturmschäden. Abkochgebote. Rohrbrüche. Das passiert. Und wenn es passiert, leiden Familien. Kinder haben Durst. Eltern geraten in Panik. Schwangere wie Julia sind gestresst und haben Angst.“ Er hat mich angesehen. „Ich hab mir gedacht: Wenn ich mich Christ nenne, dann muss ich auch bereit sein, für meine Familie zu sorgen und für die Menschen um mich herum.“ „Aber braucht man dafür nicht eine Menge Vorbereitung?“, habe ich gefragt. „Man braucht einen tragbaren Wasserfilter in Militärqualität im Auto. Das war's. Ein paar mehr hab ich zu Hause, damit ich sie in Notfällen an Leute weitergeben kann. Der ganze Aufwand ist, sie rechtzeitig zu besorgen. Aber wenn die Krise kommt, kann ich sofort helfen, statt wie alle anderen hektisch rumzurennen.“ Er hat seine Autoschlüssel rausgeholt. „Viele Christen denken, Vorsorge hat was mit Angst zu tun. Als würdest du Gott nicht zutrauen, dass er für dich sorgt. Aber ich glaube, es ist genau andersrum. Ich glaube, Gott ruft uns dazu auf, kluge Verwalter zu sein. Bereit zu sein.“ Ich habe noch in derselben Woche Filter bestellt. Nicht nur für meine Familie. Fürs Auto. Für meinen Notfallrucksack. Für meine Kinder und die Familie meiner Frau. Ich habe ein paar extra für zu Hause bestellt, damit ich, wenn die nächste Krise unsere Gemeinde trifft, einer bin, der wirklich hilft, und nicht einer, der nicht vorbereitet ist. Denn Michael hatte recht. Sorg vor für den Moment, in dem deine Familie und deine Nachbarn sofort Hilfe brauchen. Michael benutzt den HYDRO-X1 von Virest: https://virest.de/products/hydra-x1-notfall-wasserfilter-1-500-liter 60 Gramm. 1.500 Liter. Filtert jede Süßwasserquelle. Kein Strom nötig. Er hat sie im Auto, im Notfallrucksack, im Haus. Und er ist in fünf Minuten oder weniger voll einsatzbereit. Während alle anderen noch hektisch rumrennen.

Fala do 1º minuto: Beim Stromausfall in Berlin haben manche den Hahn aufgedreht und tagelang kamen nichts. Eins sagt ihr keiner. Ruhig bleiben nicht die mit dem Keller voller Wasserflaschen. Das Wasser ist nach etwa 72 Stunden weg, genau wenn die Hamsterkäufe jedes Regal im Ort leer räumen. Wer gut schläft, hat nur eins. Billiger als ein Keller voller Wasserflaschen und passt in die Tasche. So läuft ein Monat, Tag für Tag. Tag eins. Der Hahn spuckt, huste zweimal und aus. Die Straße runter leuchten schon die Handys. Abkochgebot. Keiner weiß, wann es wieder kommt. Aber ohne Strom kochst du nichts ab und das weiß jeder. Du gehst hinter's Haus, schöpst einen einmal Regenwasser von der Terrasse, steckst den Strohheim rein und trinkst. Die Hohlfasern im Bran filtet es auf dem Weg durch Poren von 0,1 Nm. Kein Warten, Kein Chemie, kein Strom. Nur in deinem Haus ändert die Warnung nichts. Tag drei. Die Läden sind leer gekauft. Du bist am Liedel vorbei gefahren und im Wasserregal war nur leere Pappe. Dabei ist überall Wasser. Der Bach hinter der Siedlung, der Pool vom Nachbarn.

Texto do anúncio: If things haven't felt crazy enough, the government has now told families to prepare and keep three critical things at home. My brother who is former special forces told me to add a fourth. I'm Jen. I'm 44. I live just outside Pensacola, Florida, with my husband Mike, our two kids, and a golden retriever who thinks the couch belongs to her. Maddie is nine. Sam is six. Our life is school drop-offs, soccer practice, and a fridge covered in drawings nobody is allowed to throw away. I'm not a prepper. I want to say that clearly, because I know how some of this is going to sound. I don't watch end-of-the-world videos. I've never owned a bucket of freeze-dried anything. Until this month, our emergency plan was a flashlight in the junk drawer that may or may not have had batteries in it. My brother Dan is the sensible one in our family. He moved to London twelve years ago for work. He lives there now with his wife and their two boys, and he works in insurance. Dan reads the fine print on everything. He checks the tire pressure before every road trip. But he is not a worrier. He's the one who tells everyone else to calm down. He thinks people who talk about the end of the world need a hobby. So when he sent me a link on a Sunday night in late September, with no message at all, I almost didn't open it. It was an interview with Britain's Defence Secretary. The man in charge of Britain's entire military had sat down with one of their biggest newspapers. And he'd told ordinary families to keep three things in the house. Some cash. A supply of bottled water. And some tinned food. Canned food, to us. The kind you can eat cold, "if your electric goes," as he put it. He listed the reasons, one after another. Cyber attacks. Power cuts. Flooding. Wildfires. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. He said he wasn't trying to scare anyone. He said most people would have these things in the cupboard already. His exact words were "alert, not alarmed." I read it twice, then texted Dan back. "That's a British thing," I wrote. "Different country, different problems." He replied with one line. "It's not a British thing. Please just do it." I didn't do it. I put a little heart on his message, made the kids' lunches for Monday, and forgot about it. I want you to remember that part, because it's the part I think about most now. Two weeks later, a storm called Isaias started building in the Gulf. At first it looked like every other storm we get this time of year. The weather people drew the cone on the map. The kids asked if school would be closed. Mike went to fill up the car. Then it got stronger. By Friday it was a hurricane, and it was heading for our stretch of coast. Isaias came ashore near Destin on the night of Friday, October 9th, as a Category 2. We're not far from there. I'll spare you most of that night. The wind sounds different when it's that strong. It doesn't howl. It roars, like a train that never finishes passing. The kids slept in our bed, and the dog wouldn't leave the hallway. Around midnight, the power went. By the next morning, more than 880,000 homes and businesses across Florida, Alabama and Georgia had no electricity. We were one of them. Nobody I know got through that storm without a story. Four people didn't get through it at all. I'm not going to pretend we had it worst. We didn't. Our roof held. Nobody was hurt. But something happened that weekend that I wasn't ready for, and it's the reason I'm writing this. It was the water. I'd always thought of a hurricane as a wind problem. Board up the windows, bring in the patio chairs, wait it out. I had never once thought of it as a water problem. On Saturday the tap was still running. I filled the kettle without thinking, the way I always do, and then remembered the stove was electric. On Sunday, the notice came through on a neighbor's phone, because ours were nearly dead. Boil water before drinking it. Our town was under a boil-water advisory. Boil it with what, I thought. Mike dug the camping stove out of the garage. It had one canister of gas left, about half full. That's when I actually counted what we had. Most of a case of the little bottles. A gallon jug in the fridge, already going warm. A couple of sports drinks the kids had forgotten about in the pantry. Maybe three gallons. For four people and a dog. In the Florida heat. With no air conditioning. We went through the first gallon by lunchtime. I wasn't even counting the dog's bowl. Mike drove to the store on Sunday afternoon. The roads were full of branches and the traffic lights were out. He came home an hour later with nothing. "No water," he said. "Not one case. People were buying sparkling water and juice and anything else that was wet." I remember standing in the kitchen in the heat, looking at the bottles lined up on the counter, and doing a kind of math I'd never done before in my life. Not money math. How many days. Sam asked for a glass of water before bed that night. I gave him half a cup and told him to sip it slowly. He's six, and he didn't understand why. I didn't want to explain it. That night, with the kids finally asleep and the whole house silent, I opened Dan's message again. "Please just do it." I called him the next morning. In London it was already the afternoon. "Are you okay?" was the first thing he said, because he'd been watching the storm on the news all weekend. I told him we were fine. I told him about the water. I told him about the half cup. He was quiet for a second. Then he said, "Did you do the three things?" "No," I said. "I didn't think it applied to us." "I did all three," he said. "And one more." I asked him why. What made a man who rolls his eyes at everything take a politician's advice so seriously. He told me it wasn't really the politician. It was that governments were all starting to say the same thing at the same time. The European Union has been telling families to keep 72 hours of food and water at home since last year. Britain is launching a whole national campaign about it this autumn. "When governments start telling people to keep water in the house," he said, "they're not guessing. They're planning. They just don't want to say it any louder than they have to." "It isn't about war," he said. "It's about everything going wrong at once. A storm. A power cut. A cyber attack on the wrong system. You don't need the end of the world. You just need one bad week." "And you just had yours," he said. Then he explained the part I'd never understood. Our tap water runs on electricity. Pumps push it through the pipes to every house. Treatment plants clean it. Computers control both. When the power goes, the pumps can go with it. When the pumps go, the pressure drops. And when the pressure drops, dirty water can get into the pipes. That's why the advisories come after storms. It isn't always a broken pipe. Sometimes it's just the power. He sent me a story from the week before. Over on the other side of Florida, a storm knocked out power to the water pumps, the pressure dropped, and families were told to boil their water before drinking it. No power. No pumps. No safe water. That's the whole chain, and it's only three links long. Then he asked me a question I still think about. "How long would your water have lasted if that advisory had gone on for two weeks?" I didn't need the math. We'd barely made it through two days. "Okay," he said. "Here's the number they don't put in the headline." The British government's own guidance says a person needs 2.5 to 3 liters of water a day just to survive. That's drinking water only. To drink, cook and keep clean, it says about 10 liters per person, per day. We're a family of four. That's 40 liters a day. About ten and a half gallons. Every single day. For three days, that's 120 liters. Over 30 gallons. Roughly five cases of gallon jugs stacked in the garage, just to get through a long weekend. My three gallons wouldn't have lasted us until lunch on day one by that standard. "That's the problem with bottled water," Dan said. "It's a countdown. Every bottle you open is one fewer. You can fill the garage and all you've done is buy a few more days. Then you're right back where you started." He walked me through it the way he walks through everything. Like an insurance claim. Option one. Buy more bottled water. It helps, and you should have some. But it's heavy, it fills the garage, and you can't take it with you if you have to leave. A week of water for a family our size weighs about 600 pounds. Option two. Boil it. That works, as long as the power is on or the gas is on. Which is exactly the moment you don't have them. Option three. Go to the store. We'd tried that. "So what's the fourth thing?" I asked him. He laughed. "I wondered when you'd ask. It isn't more water. It's a way to make more." He keeps a small hollow-fiber water filter in the kitchen drawer. One in the car. One in each of his boys' school bags. Each one about the size of a flashlight. "The three things get you through a few days," he said. "This is what you need when a few days isn't enough." I'll be honest, my first reaction was the same as it had been to the article. A filter? Like the camping ones? So I sat down and read. The good portable filters use something called a hollow-fiber membrane. Picture thousands of tiny straws packed side by side, each one thinner than a hair. The walls of those little straws are full of microscopic holes. The holes are about 0.1 microns wide. That's so small that bacteria and parasites physically can't fit through. They get trapped on the outside. Clean water passes through to the inside. To give you an idea of how small that is, a single E. coli bacterium is roughly one to two microns long. Giardia, a parasite that causes a lot of the stomach illness people get from untreated water, is around ten microns across. That's about a hundred times wider than the holes it would need to squeeze through. It isn't a chemical killing anything. It's more like a sieve so fine that the things that make you sick simply can't get to the other side. No chemicals. No electricity. No batteries. Just the size of the hole. I asked Dan the obvious question. We already have a filter on the fridge, and a pitcher filter on the counter. Doesn't that do the same thing? It doesn't. Most of those are carbon filters. They're designed to make tap water that's already been treated taste better, by taking out chlorine and odors. You can drink straight through one like a straw. Or you can attach it to a bottle and squeeze the water through. Which means almost any freshwater you can get to becomes drinking water. You fill the bag or bottle with water from wherever you are, screw the filter on, and squeeze or sip. When it starts to slow down, you push a little clean water back through it with a syringe to flush it out, and it flows again. There's nothing to set up and nothing to plug in. I want it to be normal. I also did the three things. The cash is in an envelope in the safe. The canned food is on the bottom shelf of the pantry. And yes, we have bottled water now too. The bottles are for the first few days. The filters are for everything after. Then I thought about our mom. She's 71. She lives on her own, about an hour from us, in a little house with a big garden she won't give up. She takes her pills every morning with a glass of water from the tap. During the storm, I couldn't reach her for most of a day. The phones were down. When I finally got through, she told me she'd been drinking the water from the tap the whole time. She hadn't heard about the advisory. She was fine. But I sat in my car afterward and shook. Dan sent her one the same week. She keeps it in the kitchen drawer next to her tea towels, where she'll actually see it. My neighbor across the street saw the box on our porch and asked what it was. I told her the whole story standing in the driveway. She ordered two before I'd finished. That's the thing about going through a week like that. More than half a million people in the streets in a single day. Over a thousand arrests. Shops broken into in Paris, Marseille, Nice, and city after city. I'm not saying that's coming here. I want to say that clearly, because I know how some of this is going to sound. I don't watch end-of-the-world videos. I've never owned a bucket of freeze-dried anything. Until this month, our emergency plan was a flashlight in the junk drawer that may or may not have had batteries in it. My brother Dan is the sensible one in our family. He moved to London twelve years ago for work. He lives there now with his wife and their two boys, and he works in insurance. Dan reads the fine print on everything. He checks the tire pressure before every road trip. But he is not a worrier. He's the one who tells everyone else to calm down. He thinks people who talk about the end of the world need a hobby. So when he sent me a link on a Sunday night in late September, with no message at all, I almost didn't open it. It was an interview with Britain's Defence Secretary. The man in charge of Britain's entire military had sat down with one of their biggest newspapers. And he'd told ordinary families to keep three things in the house. Some cash. A supply of bottled water. And some tinned food. Canned food, to us. The kind you can eat cold, "if your electric goes," as he put it. He listed the reasons, one after another. Cyber attacks. Power cuts. Flooding. Wildfires. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. He said he wasn't trying to scare anyone. He said most people would have these things in the cupboard already. The kids slept in our bed, and the dog wouldn't leave the hallway. Around midnight, the power went. By the next morning, more than 880,000 homes and businesses across Florida, Alabama and Georgia had no electricity. We were one of them. Nobody I know got through that storm without a story. Four people didn't get through it at all. I'm not going to pretend we had it worst. We didn't. Our roof held. Nobody was hurt. Mike drove to the store on Sunday afternoon. The roads were full of branches and the traffic lights were out. He came home an hour later with nothing. "No water," he said. "Not one case. Texto do anúncio: Zwei Wohnzimmer. Derselbe Stromausfall. Links: Alle sitzen im Dunkeln. Das Handy ist fast leer, das Netz weg. Keiner weiß, was los ist. Rechts: Licht im Raum, das Radio läuft, die Kinder hören zu. Papa hat vorgesorgt. Der Unterschied ist kein Notstromaggregat. Es ist ein Gerät, das in die Küchenschublade passt: das 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗼. Warum gerade ein Radio? Wenn der Strom ausfällt, laufen die Handymasten nur kurz auf Notstrom. Rundfunksender sind für den Ernstfall abgesichert. Über sie kommen die Durchsagen: wie lange es dauert, wo es Hilfe gibt, was zu tun ist. Deshalb steht ein Radio, das ohne Steckdose läuft, ausdrücklich auf der Checkliste des Bundesamts für Bevölkerungsschutz. ✅ 𝗨𝗞𝗪- 𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗪-𝗥𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗼: genau die Sender, über die im Ernstfall Durchsagen kommen ✅ 𝗛𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗟𝗘𝗗-𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗻𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗲: Licht ohne Kerzen und ohne Brandrisiko für die Kinder ✅ 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗸-𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗸𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: aus dem 2.000-mAh-Akku das Handy nachladen ✅ 𝗟𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝗵𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘀𝗲: per Handkurbel oder über das Solarpanel ✅ Kompakt für Küchenschublade, Notfallrucksack oder Auto ⭐ 4,8 von 5 Sternen aus 273 Bewertungen 🛡️ Geld-zurück-Garantie Ein Tipp: Leg es dorthin, wo du es auch im Dunkeln findest. Texto do anúncio: Kein Strom? Dann zählen drei Dinge. ✔ Licht, damit du dich im Dunkeln zurechtfindest ✔ Radio, damit du weißt, was los ist ✔ Strom fürs Handy, damit du erreichbar bleibst Die meisten Haushalte haben dafür, wenn überhaupt, drei verschiedene Dinge: eine Taschenlampe mit alten Batterien, ein Küchenradio an der Steckdose und eine Powerbank, die längst leer ist. “Siate pronti in caso di emergenza!”
🎙 “Quando i governi europei cominciano a mettere guide di sopravvivenza nelle cassette delle lettere, non è per caso. E se stai pensando di pre”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: Non fare lo stesso errore del 90% delle persone. Pensano di essere pronte. Poi salta la corrente. Buio totale. Niente rete. Nessuna informazione. E lì ti rendi conto di una cosa: Non hai alcun controllo. Una torcia? Senza pile, inutile. Un powerbank? Scarico in poche ore. Uno smartphone? Inutile senza rete. Ti hanno venduto soluzioni che dipendono da qualcos’altro. Il vero problema di un blackout non è solo l’elettricità. 35 dias
“sem título”
🎙 “Si je devais garder qu'un seul équipement d'urgence, ce serait celui-ci. La plupart des gens se trompe sur l'audurgence.”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: L’eau du robinet est contrôlée en France. Mais “conforme” ne veut pas dire “toujours garantie”. 💧 Ces dernières années, des millions de Français ont reçu au moins une fois une eau non conforme à cause des pesticides et de leurs résidus. À Mayotte, l’eau est rationnée depuis 2023, et les autorités déconseillent de la boire juste après une coupure. Et en cas de vraie crise, l’eau est la première chose qui manque. C’est pour ça que le gouvernement recommande à chaque foyer de préparer un kit de secours pour tenir 72 heures, avec au minimum 6 litres d’eau par personne. L’AQUA-GS1 est le complément idéal à ce kit : ✅ Filtre l’eau d’un ruisseau, d’un étang ou d’un bidon de récupération grâce à la gravité ✅ Membrane 0,1 micron : bactéries, parasites et microplastiques ✅ Aucune électricité, aucune pile : impossible de te “couper” l’eau ✅ Léger, se range dans un placard ou un sac à dos Un stock d’eau en bouteille se vide. Un filtre, lui, te donne accès à l’eau tant qu’il y a une source.
Fala do 1º minuto: Si je devais garder qu'un seul équipement d'urgence, ce serait celui-ci. La plupart des gens se trompe sur l'audurgence. Stokes ça ne marche pas. Une famille vide un pack d'eau plus vite qu'on croit et impossible dans stokes assez pour une vraie crise. La solution n'est pas de stokes et l'eau, mais de la rendre potable à la demande, depuis n'importe quel source apporté. C'est ça la filtration par gravité. La coassure vit, utilise une membrane à fibres creuse de 0,1 microns, assez fine pour bloquer physiquement bactéries par asite, protozoaires et microplastiques. 99,49% bloqués, testés en l'abo et aucune énergie requise. Pas de pilapla, pas de produits chimiques à racheter, pas d'électricité, juste la gravité qui marche avec ou sans courant. Un seul filtre vous donne jusqu'à 3 800 litres, pas quelques jours d'eau, mais des moins d'eau potable pour votre famille. À la demande, cliquez-y dessous et essayez la coassure vit sans risque pendant 90 jours. Installez-le, testez-le et voyez par vous-même l'eau propre qui en sort.

8 dias
“Parents, grands-parents : lisez ceci 👆”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: Mon fils ne m'a posé qu'une question. C'était le soir du 13 février, dans mon garage, à la clarté d'une frontale. Dehors, le groupe électrogène tournait pour le congélateur. Thomas, accroupi devant mon étagère, celle dont je suis le plus fier, comptait à voix haute les packs d'eau rangés tout en bas. « Un, deux, trois, quatre. » Puis il s'est relevé, il m'a fixé et il m'a demandé : « Et après les packs, Papa ? » Je n'ai pas su quoi lui répondre. Moi qui ai une réponse à tout dans ce garage. Je m'appelle Patrick, j'ai 59 ans. J'ai été électricien à mon compte 34 ans dans les Landes, dans un village entre Mont-de-Marsan et la forêt. J'ai câblé des maisons, des fermes, des pompes de forage, et pas mal d'armoires électriques pour les stations de pompage du coin. J'ai vendu l'affaire il y a deux ans, à cause du dos. Martine, ma femme, dit que depuis, c'est le garage qui a pris ma place. Elle n'a pas tort. Il faut que je vous explique d'où ça vient. En janvier 2009, la tempête Klaus a coupé l'électricité de plus de 1,7 million de foyers dans le Sud-Ouest. Autour du village, les pins étaient couchés partout. J'ai passé des semaines à rebrancher des gens, du matin jusqu'à la nuit, et j'ai vu des familles entières se débrouiller avec trois bougies et une boîte d'allumettes. Je me suis promis que ça ne nous arriverait pas. Alors j'ai tout prévu. En 17 ans, j'ai monté l'étagère dont rêverait n'importe quel artisan : des lampes de toutes les tailles, une radio à manivelle, des piles rangées par format dans des boîtes transparentes, des bougies, trois semaines de conserves, un réchaud, une trousse de secours. Et un groupe électrogène que je révise chaque automne. Au mur, une liste au crayon que je coche au fur et à mesure. Lampes, coché. Piles, coché. Conserves, coché. En bas de l'étagère, 4 packs d'eau. Je les changeais tous les ans. Pour moi, l'eau, c'était réglé. Puis il y a eu Nils. En février 2026, la tempête Nils a coupé le courant à près de 900 000 foyers dans le Sud-Ouest. Thomas, notre fils, qui a 31 ans et qui vit à Bordeaux, était descendu la veille avec Camille, sa compagne, pour nous aider à attacher tout ce qui pouvait s'envoler. Nous étions donc 4 à la maison quand le vent s'est levé. La nuit du 11 au 12, on a entendu les pins craquer derrière la maison. Vers 2 heures du matin, tout s'est éteint. Au lever du jour, il y avait des branches partout dans la cour et un pin couché en travers du fossé, au fond du terrain. Et là, je vous le dis honnêtement, j'étais content de moi. Le groupe a démarré au premier coup. Le congélateur tournait, la radio donnait les nouvelles, chacun avait sa lampe. Martine a fait chauffer l'eau du café sur le réchaud. Camille m'a dit : « Patrick, on est mieux ici qu'à l'hôtel. » J'ai fait semblant de ne pas être fier. Le deuxième jour, la pression a commencé à baisser au robinet. Un filet qui crachotait. Et autour de nous, personne ne savait dire si on pouvait encore la boire. Ça, j'aurais dû le voir venir, plus que n'importe qui. L'eau du robinet, ce n'est pas un tuyau branché sur une source : elle est pompée, traitée, puis poussée dans les canalisations par des moteurs électriques. J'en ai câblé, de ces moteurs. Quand le courant manque assez longtemps sur un secteur, les pompes s'arrêtent et la pression tombe. Mon groupe faisait tourner mon congélateur. Pas les pompes qui amènent l'eau jusque chez moi. Je le savais. Je ne l'avais simplement jamais relié à ma propre étagère. C'est ce soir-là que Thomas a compté les packs. 4 packs de 6 bouteilles d'un litre et demi, ça fait 36 litres. Le guide officiel de préparation aux crises recommande d'avoir 6 litres d'eau par personne pour tenir 72 heures. Pour nous 4, ça fait 24 litres, et ça ne compte que l'eau qu'on boit. Thomas a continué le calcul à voix haute : le café, les pâtes, la vaisselle, se brosser les dents, se laver un minimum. « Compte une dizaine de litres par personne et par jour, Papa. À 4, ça fait 40 litres. Tes packs, c'est une journée. » C'est là qu'il m'a posé sa question. Je suis resté devant ma liste, le crayon à la main. Tout en bas, j'ai écrit : « Eau ? » Avec un point d'interrogation. C'était la première fois en 17 ans que j'ajoutais une ligne à cette liste sans pouvoir la cocher. Thomas n'a rien dit de plus. Il est sorti jusqu'à sa voiture, et il est revenu avec son sac de randonnée. Il faut savoir que Thomas part bivouaquer dans les Pyrénées plusieurs week-ends par an. Je l'ai toujours un peu chambré avec ça. Il a sorti de son sac une poche bleue pliée, un petit filtre et un tuyau. « C'est avec ça que je bois là-haut, il m'a dit. Je ne porte pas l'eau. Je la fais. » Au réveil, il m'a emmené au fond du terrain. Derrière la maison, il y a une craste, un de ces fossés qu'on creuse chez nous pour drainer la forêt. Après la tempête, elle était pleine à ras bord. Une eau marron, quasiment couleur café au lait, avec des aiguilles de pin qui flottaient et un peu de mousse sur le bord. Le genre d'eau que je n'aurais pas donnée au chien. Thomas a rempli la poche, il l'a accrochée à une branche du pin tombé, il a branché le tuyau et il a mis la poche propre en dessous. Quelques secondes, rien. Puis l'eau a commencé à descendre, goutte à goutte d'abord, puis en un filet régulier. Pas de moteur, pas de bruit. Moi qui ai passé ma vie à faire tourner des pompes, je regardais de l'eau arriver sans un seul fil électrique. En haut, l'eau de la craste. En dessous, de l'eau claire. Thomas m'a tendu un verre. Je l'ai senti d'abord, par réflexe. Aucune odeur de fossé. Et j'ai bu. De l'eau. Fraîche, normale, sans goût de terre ni de sable. Le midi, Martine a fait le café avec. Camille a hésité un moment devant sa tasse, puis elle en a redemandé une deuxième. Thomas m'a montré le nom du kit : l'AQUA-GS1. Une poche de 3,8 litres qu'on remplit dans un fossé, une mare, une rivière, une cuve ou un récupérateur d'eau de pluie. Pour un mécanicien, c'est quasiment vexant : il n'y a rien qui puisse tomber en panne. Un seul filtre traite jusqu'à 5 700 litres. J'ai fait le calcul plus tard : pour Martine et moi, plus de 2 ans d'eau à boire. Je n'y croyais pas une seconde. Alors on a fait le test, là, aussitôt, avec la pire eau du jardin. J'ai plongé le seau dans la cuve du milieu, celle qui prend le plus le soleil. L'eau était vert pâle, avec des feuilles de noyer qui flottaient et un dépôt brun au fond. Jeannot a rempli la poche, il l'a accrochée au clou de la porte de la grange et il a ouvert le petit robinet du filtre. Quelques secondes, rien. Puis l'eau a commencé à couler, lentement, en silence. En haut, elle était verte. En dessous, elle était claire. Martine est sortie de la cuisine avec un verre. Elle l'a levé à la clarté, elle l'a senti longtemps, puis elle a bu une toute petite gorgée. Et elle a dit : « Elle a le goût de l'eau. » Rien de plus. Mais je l'ai vue souffler, comme quand on pose un sac trop lourd. J'ai bu à mon tour. Fraîche, sans goût de vase, sans goût de rien. De l'eau. Ce soir-là, j'ai commandé le nôtre. Et j'en ai commandé un deuxième pour Raymonde et Lucien. Quand le colis est arrivé, je suis allé l'installer chez eux. J'ai vissé un crochet sous l'avancée de leur appentis, juste à côté du récupérateur, à hauteur de main, pour que Raymonde n'ait pas à grimper sur un escabeau. Je lui ai montré deux fois. La deuxième fois, c'est elle qui l'a fait. Lucien regardait l'eau couler et il a soupiré : « Et dire qu'on a porté des packs. » L'eau est revenue au robinet le sixième jour, avec un papier dans la boîte aux lettres qui disait de la faire bouillir encore quelques jours. Chez nous, on n'a pas eu besoin. Je ne prétends pas que votre robinet va s'arrêter demain. Personne ne peut le savoir, et je ne suis pas là pour faire peur. Je raconte ce qui s'est passé chez nous, dans un coin de campagne où personne n'aurait cru manquer d'eau un jour. Et si vous avez un puits, une cuve ou un récupérateur, vous avez déjà fait le plus dur : l'eau, vous l'avez. Il vous manque seulement de quoi la rendre buvable. Le premier soir avec le kit, Martine a fait le café avec l'eau de la cuve. Elle l'a posé sur la table sans rien dire et elle a attendu que je goûte. Je n'ai rien remarqué. Une chose quand même, pour être honnête : si vous voulez boire l'eau de votre puits tous les jours, faites-la analyser, ça reste le bon réflexe. Le kit, c'est pour les jours où le robinet s'arrête. En ce moment, c'est le Black Friday : 59,99 € le kit, le 2e à moitié prix, 3 guides de survie offerts, la livraison offerte et 90 jours satisfait ou remboursé. Jusqu'au 30 novembre. Voici le lien : https://aquasecours.com/products/kit-de-survie-aqua-gs1 Aujourd'hui, l'eau de notre jardin, on peut la boire.

A potem pewnej nocy przeglądałem fora surwiwalowy i dotarło do mnie, że popełniłam cztery kluczowe błędy, które mogłyby mnie zabić już w pierwszym tygodni. I widzę, że mnóstwo ludzi robić dziś dokładnie to samo. Błąd numer jeden. Gromadzenie zapasów jedzenia na lata, ale brak jakiegokolwiek zapasowego źródła energii. Masz piwnice pełną słoików, konserw gotowego jedzenia podsufit, ale kiedy padnie się, nie widzisz nic. Nie nładujesz radia, żeby wiedzieć co się dzieje. Nie skontaktujesz się z nimi. To całe jedzenie niewiele znaczek, gdy siedzisz w totalnej ciemności bez informacji, zastanawiasz się, czy w ogóle bezpiecznie jest wyjść na zerność. Błąd numer dwa. Poleganie na agregatach, które ogłaszają całej okolicy, że masz zapas. W momencie, gdy odpalaż głównie agregat prądotwórczy, każda nieprzygotowana osoba w pobliżu, wie, gdzie iść, kiedy zrobi się naprawdę źle. To jak wystawienie szyldu, mamy prąd i zapasy. Zapraszamy. Zabierzcie nam przyz...

ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: Co zabierzesz, gdy o 3 w nocy trzeba wyjść z bloku? Na pakowanie masz kilka minut, a w głowie chaos... Poznaj plecak ewakuacyjny „Ewakuacja” – gotowy zestaw na pierwsze 72 godziny, który czeka przy drzwiach. ✅ Namiot termiczny, koc i saperka – schronienie w kilka minut ✅ Oświetlenie survivalowe 3w1 i czołówka – światło, gdy pada prąd ✅ Pełna apteczka i zestaw survivalowy 32w1 – ogień, woda, jedzenie ✅ Radio na korbkę i multitool – wszystko w jednym plecaku przy drzwiach ❗ GRATIS: e-book „Pierwsze 72 godziny” + darmowa dostawa Black Weeks trwa tylko do 30.11. Zamów plecak ewakuacyjny już dziś i śpij spokojnie. 👉 Link na dole.
Fala do 1º minuto: Pytacie co powinien zawierać dobry plecak ewakuacyjny? Już pokazuje. Po pierwsze pełna apteczka, żeby od razu zająć się bliskimi. Do tego namiot i kod sermiczny, saperka i multitool. Oświetlenie surwiwalowe 3-1 i radiona korbkę, bo w czasie kryzysu prąd pada jako pierwszy. Zesta w surwiwalowy 32-1. Potnież drewno na opał i rozpalisz ognisko. A z zestawem dołowienia ryb nie martwisz się o jedzenie. Dokładasz tylko dokumenty i wodę i jesteś gotowy na pierwsze trzydowy. W naszym plecaku to wszystko już jest. Zamówisz zapobraniem, a poradnik na 72-dw. dostajesz gratis.

🎙 “Nous ritures, au potable, pile et argent liquide, pourquoi les gouvernements du monde entier demandent soudainement ? Alors citoyens d'être ”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: La France a publié sa liste : de quoi tenir 72 heures seul chez soi. Coupure de courant, tempête, inondation. La plupart des foyers n’ont rien de prêt. Notre kit reprend la liste officielle, déjà rangée dans un sac 25 L avec trois sacs étanches. Vous ajoutez l’eau, la nourriture et vos médicaments, et c’est prêt. L’hiver arrive. C’est maintenant qu’on s’équipe, pas le soir où tout s’éteint.
Fala do 1º minuto: Nous ritures, au potable, pile et argent liquide, pourquoi les gouvernements du monde entier demandent soudainement ? Alors citoyens d'être prêt à servir 72 heures, seul, parce que oui, des États-Unis, au Japon, passant par l'Angleterre et même des préfectures en France, tu peux le voir, haute-signement, les consignes en fait de quittre d'urgence tombant boucle. Moi, ma question, je veux pas me faire paniquer, on panique pas mais qu'est-ce qu'on nous prépare ? Parce que regardez ce qui se passe un peu sous nos yeux sans faire trop de bruit, on a en France en fait que ministère de l'Intérieur et plusieurs préfects qui multiplient des campagnes pour inciter en fait chaque foyer à constituer un type de la banque. C'est comme ça qu'ils appellent ça. Si l'itre d'eau per personne, des boîtes de conserve, radio à pile et une trousse de secours et du cache bien sûr, sous le mat là. On a le même son de cloche chez les américains avec la FEM appardant et au Japon avec leur protocole de crise et au Royaume-Uni il y a quelques jours. Donc on nous répète en fait en boucle, la réglue du jeu, en cas de paie pas les sous-cornétales ne viennent, on ne pas frapper à votre porte avant, au moins trois jours, donc bonne chance et démerdez-vous. Alors maintenant, posons-nous un peu la question qu'achet. Pourquoi cette panique préventive à l'échelle internationale ?

32 dias
“Corso di Sopravvivenza 28-29 Novembre 2026 - Civita (CS)”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: Corso di Sopravvivenza 1° Livello FISSS 28-29 Novembre 2026 - Civita (CS) Per informazioni e prenotazioni puoi scrivere su Whatsapp al 3476321594 oppure a info@sos2012.it SURVIVAL SCHOOL SOS2012 è SCUOLA FEDERALE MASTER FISSS (Federazione Italiana Survival Sportivo e Sperimentale) e riconosciuta ufficialmente dal CONI, da ASI NAZIONALE e MSP Settore Survival Bushcraft, che si avvale solo di Istruttori professionisti con riconoscimento Federale ed europeo CERTIFICATI INTERNAZIONALI EURETHICS/ETSIA e CONI. Al termine del corso verrà rilasciato un attestato di partecipazione riconosciuto ASI e FISSS. l corso si terrà all'interno della splendida cornice boschiva del Bosco delle Fate di Civita (CS) Il Corso di sopravvivenza di 1° Livello (fondamentale per accedere agli altri tipi di Corsi) è l'esperienza di Survival dedicata a chi per la prima volta si avvicina a questo tipo di disciplina e/o vuole anche intraprendere la strada formativa per diventare ISTRUTTORE di Sopravvivenza Federale FISSS. Verranno insegnate e testate varie tecniche e linee guida utili al sostentamento del singolo o del gruppo, non soltanto in situazioni di emergenza o calamità naturali, ma anche come conoscenze a supporto di normali attività sportive ed outdoor: trekking, mountain bike , equitazione, caccia e pesca. Una formazione e una filosofia volta a riscoprire le innate capacità umane di adattamento e di Problem Solving, conosciute e tramandate per secoli dai nostri antenati. "RISCOPRENDO LA NATURA RITROVEREMO NOI STESSI e le antiche conoscenze innate ma sepolte in ognuno di noi". Wolfman I nostri Istruttori professionisti FISSS, certificati anche CONI, Ministero Sport e Salute, ASI Settore Survival Bushcraft, con esperienza ventennale, vi guideranno alla costruzione di un riparo di fortuna per il pernottamento, all'accensione di un fuoco con tecniche primitive. Inoltre la scuola nodi ci permetterà di conoscerli e saperli utilizzare in ogni emergenza e nella costruzione del riparo stesso. Impareremo ad utilizzare le Lame e gli utensili in modo corretto. Affronteremo un dirupo con le corde in modo sicuro. Impareremo a riconoscere le piante commestibili ed officinali e come realizzare un kit di sopravvivenza personale (DIFFIDATE SEMPRE DEI KIT SOPRAVVIVENZA PRECONFEZIONATI), come orientarci con e senza bussola di giorno e di notte ed altre interessanti attività, per poter vivere in ambiente outdoor con sicurezza e divertimento e nel rispetto della Natura ed imparare al tempo stesso come cavarcela in ogni situazione di emergenza e criticità. Non sono dunque previste in alcun modo tende e sacchi a pelo e generi alimentari portati dall'esterno. Preferiamo farveli realizzare e trovare come se fosse in una situazione di reale emergenza. Impareremo a costruire armi primitive (arco, lancia, frombola, fionda ecc) e a realizzare trappole (ovviamente simulate) e tantissime altre attività presenti sul programma. Se sei solo non preoccuparti, il gruppo lo facciamo noi. Se avrai un weekend libero, potrai gratuitamente partecipare ai Corsi di Sopravvivenza di 1° Livello successivi in modo da ripetere e approfondire le tecniche acquisite ed eventualmente testare equipaggiamenti e insegnamenti in totale autonomia e partecipare a tutte le attività della scuola (raduni, viaggi avventura, spedizioni, escursioni, sopralluoghi). Il corso è articolato su due giorni, sabato e domenica ed ha un costo di 130€ comprensivi di: quota e tessera associativa, fornitura dell'attrezzatura necessaria, Dispense didattiche e inserimento nei Gruppi online Ufficiali (che vi consentiranno di rimanere sempre in contatto con noi), diploma di partecipazione al corso ed un coltello SURVIVAL Mora of SWEDEN con logo inciso SOS2012®, che rimarrà tuo! Il corso di sopravvivenza di primo livello è propedeutico alla frequentazione del secondo livello (intermedio) ed è valido per accedere al percorso professionale della FISSS (Federazione Italiana Survival Sportivo e Sperimentale) in qualità di "Supporter". Non è necessaria alcuna precedente esperienza. IL CORSO E' A NUMERO CHIUSO. Questo Corso di Sopravvivenza è certificato ISO/IEC 17024. Significa che la formazione proposta dalla SOS2012 viene riconosciuta all’interno di un sistema che pone al centro qualità, competenza, trasparenza e affidabilità. Per informazioni e prenotazioni puoi scrivere su Whatsapp al 3476321594 oppure a info@sos2012.it

“Corso Scheggiatura Selce”
ver texto e fala completos
Texto do anúncio: Corso Scheggiatura della Selce e Immanicatura 19-20 Dicembre 2026 - Roio (AQ) Luogo: Roio (AQ) presso la Scuola delle Piante e dei Mestieri Costo: 120€ Durata: 2 giorni, Sabato e Domenica (dalle ore 8,30 alle ore 16,30 circa) Per informazioni ed iscrizioni potete contattarci tramite whatsapp al 3476321594 oppure scriverci a info@sos2012.it CORSO PER MAX. 12 PERSONE Al termine del corso verrà rilasciato un attestato di partecipazione riconosciuto dal RUNTS. SURVIVAL SCHOOL SOS2012® è SCUOLA FEDERALE FISSS (Federazione Italiana Survival Sportivo e Sperimentale) e riconosciuta ufficialmente dal Ministero Sport e Salute e dall'ASI, con Istruttori certificati internazionali EURETHICS/ETSIA, inoltre, è una APS iscritta la Terzo Settore presso ASI. La scheggiatura della selce iniziò nel Paleolitico, circa 3 milioni di anni fa, con l'Homo Habilis che creò i primi strumenti taglienti, come il chopper. Attraverso questa tecnica di percussione o pressione, l'uomo otteneva schegge di selce, ossidiana e altre pietre con frattura concoide, creando poi utensili sempre più raffinati come lame, punte e raschiatoi. Questo corso è pensato per tutti. Non sono necessarie esperienze pregresse. Appassionati di archeologia sperimentale, survivalisti, educatori ambientali, artigiani o semplici curiosi desiderosi di toccare con mano una delle tecnologie più antiche dell’umanità. Ecco alcuni degli argomenti che verranno trattati: Giorno 1 Questo primo giorno di corso offre un’introduzione completa all’antica arte della scheggiatura litica. L’obiettivo è fornire le basi teoriche e pratiche per creare un kit litico di sopravvivenza. Parte teorica (9:00 – 10:30): Verranno affrontate le origini della tecnologia litica preistorica, il riconoscimento delle materie prime (selce, ossidiana, quarzo), i principi base della scheggiatura e la terminologia fondamentale (scheggia, nucleo). Parte pratica (10:30 – 16:00/17:00): I partecipanti avranno l’opportunità di fare pratica direttamente sulla materia prima, utilizzando strumenti di lavorazione, sperimentando tecniche come la percussione diretta, la bipolare e il ritocco, con l’obiettivo di creare strumenti a margine tagliente, lame seghettate e punte. La fase finale del corso prevede la sperimentazione di questi strumenti su materiali come legno, osso, pelle e carne, dimostrando che “niente è uno scarto” e tutto può essere utile alla sopravvivenza. Giorno 2 Parte pratica (8:30 – 16:00/17:00) Il secondo giorno di corso offre un’esperienza più approfondita, combinando la scheggiatura con la creazione di strumenti compositi. Partendo da una delle schegge prodotte e avvalendosi del kit realizzato il giorno precedente, i partecipanti impareranno a creare un manico su misura utilizzando legno, a preparare il cordino con la fibra vegetale e a sigillare il tutto con il bitume. L’obiettivo è di acquisire le competenze necessarie per assemblare in autonomia uno strumento funzionale e robusto, unendo le abilità di scheggiatura con la tecnologia composita per creare oggetti indispensabili per la sopravvivenza. Per informazioni e prenotazioni scrivi su Whatsapp al 3476321594 oppure tramite email a info@sos2012.it
